domains.name: The Deep Work Study Protocol
domains.summary: How the site teaches: the curriculum as an attention delivery system — distraction-free design, the one-module rhythm, attention training, artifact metrics, and slow-productivity pacing.

scenarios.title: The Device Rules
scenarios.situation: Leo opens a 90-minute study module with his phone on the desk (notifications on), twelve tabs open, and a group chat pinging. He reads the whole module and feels he 'studied.'
scenarios.prompt: What does the protocol say about his side of the bargain?
choices: He broke it. The site holds up its end by never manufacturing a distraction — no feed, no recommendations, no autoplay — and the protocol asks the learner to hold up theirs: notifications off, phone in another room, one tab open. The page cannot silence his phone; the device rules are his half of the design.
His setup is fine — willpower handles notifications.
The protocol only governs the site's design, not the learner.
He should study on his phone instead, since it's always with him.
scenarios.why: Distraction-free by design is a two-party contract. The curriculum is engineered as a delivery system for sustained attention — long-form pages, no engagement machinery, the page you opened is the page you study — but it assumes the device rules from the deep-work track. A site that never distracts you plus a phone that constantly does is still a distracted session.
scenarios.hint: Which half of the contract did Leo keep?

scenarios.title: One Module, One Session
scenarios.situation: Aisha has 45 minutes before work. She opens a module, skims half, switches to another track's module for variety, then answers email 'while she's at it.' She logs 'two modules touched.'
scenarios.prompt: Apply the study rhythm.
choices: Wrong rhythm on every axis: one module, one deep session. A module is a single long-form page because the material is cognitively demanding and needs unbroken time — she should have done one module fully (or none), with the session ending when the module ends. Half-modules and interleaved tracks are how dependency chains break.
Her approach is efficient — variety keeps the brain fresh.
She should have skimmed faster to finish both modules.
Email during study is fine if the replies are short.
scenarios.why: The study rhythm is one module, one deep session: the page's length is deliberate, the session's boundary is the module's end, and switching tracks mid-session is attention residue by design. 'Modules touched' is a vanity metric; the rhythm exists so each module's prerequisites are actually met before the next builds on them.
scenarios.hint: What will Aisha have built by the end of those 45 minutes?

scenarios.title: Hours vs. Artifacts
scenarios.situation: Two learners report their month. Ben logged 120 study hours (videos watched, pages scrolled). Cara logged 40 hours — and produced 12 lab artifacts, 4 re-derived proofs, and a working project.
scenarios.prompt: Who does the protocol judge as further along?
choices: Cara, unambiguously. Depth metrics: done means artifacts, not hours. Hours measure exposure; artifacts measure capability. Ben has 120 hours of familiarity; Cara has 40 hours of evidence — and only evidence compounds into the next module's prerequisites.
Ben — 120 hours is three times the effort.
Tie — both put in real work.
Ben, because consistency of hours predicts long-term success.
scenarios.why: The protocol's metric commitment is explicit: artifacts, not hours. A lab completed, a proof re-derived by hand, a fuzzer that found a real bug — these are the units of done. Hours are input; artifacts are output. Any system that rewards the input gets the input optimized and the output faked.
scenarios.hint: If both applied for the same role tomorrow, whose evidence would you hire on?

scenarios.title: The Sprint-and-Burn Semester
scenarios.situation: A study group plans their semester: ignore the material for ten weeks, then a two-week cram sprint before finals — energy drinks, all-nighters, twelve-hour days.
scenarios.prompt: What does slow-productivity pacing prescribe instead?
choices: The opposite arc: fewer obligations carried at once, work at a natural pace across the whole semester, obsessive focus on quality per module — one module per deep session, artifacts as gates. Sustainable depth beats sprint-and-burn because attention is trainable only under consistent load, and cramming produces familiarity that evaporates before the final that matters: actual capability.
The sprint plan is fine — pressure produces focus.
Extend the sprint to three weeks for safety.
Cramming works if you take good notes during the sprint.
scenarios.why: Slow productivity is the pacing layer of the protocol: do fewer things, at a natural pace, obsessing over quality. It is not slowness for its own sake — it is the recognition that depth compounds and cramming doesn't. A semester paced this way ends with artifacts; a sprint ends with exhaustion and evaporating familiarity.
scenarios.hint: What will the group remember — and be able to do — four weeks after the sprint?

scenarios.title: Auditing a Curriculum
scenarios.situation: You're asked to audit a commercial course platform against the five commitments: distraction-free by design, the study rhythm, attention training in the curriculum, depth metrics, and slow-productivity pacing. The platform has autoplay, infinite recommendations, streak counters, and 'completion' for watching videos.
scenarios.prompt: What is your audit verdict?
choices: It fails all five, structurally. Autoplay and recommendations manufacture the fragmentation the protocol forbids; streak counters reward hours and clicks instead of artifacts; video-watch 'completion' inverts the depth metric; and the engagement machinery makes slow, deliberate pacing impossible. The platform is engineered against the learner — every mechanism that keeps users on the platform fragments the attention the material requires.
It passes — engagement features help learners stay motivated.
It passes four of five; only the metrics need tweaking.
The audit is inconclusive without A/B test data.
scenarios.why: The five commitments are a checklist you can hold any curriculum to — including this site. Distraction-free design means the missing features are missing deliberately; the rhythm means modules are session-sized; attention training means the curriculum teaches focus as a skill; depth metrics mean artifacts gate progress; pacing means the arc is sustainable. A platform optimized for engagement cannot satisfy them, because engagement and attention are competing objectives.
scenarios.hint: Which of the five could survive autoplay? Which couldn't?

scenarios.title: Your Own Protocol
scenarios.situation: After studying the protocol, you want to run your own study life on the same five commitments for the next 90 days — across job-hunt prep, a certification track, and an open-source project.
scenarios.prompt: What does a complete personal protocol specify?
choices: All five, operationalized: the environment contract (device rules, one tab, phone away — your half of the bargain); the rhythm (one module per deep session, session ends when the module ends); attention training (weekly deep-hour targets that ratchet up, boredom tolerance practice); the metric (artifact quotas per week, hours explicitly not counted); and the pacing (fixed shutdown, sustainable weekly load, quarterly review of artifacts produced). Plus the review loop that holds you to it.
A stricter app blocker and longer study hours.
Copying the site's track pages exactly as your schedule.
Studying whenever motivation strikes, but with the phone away.
scenarios.why: The protocol is stated publicly so learners can hold the site to it — and run their own study life on the same rules. A personal protocol needs each commitment as a mechanism, not an aspiration: environment rules, session boundaries, training targets, artifact quotas, pacing guardrails, and a review that checks the artifacts. Ninety days of that is a different education than ninety days of hours.
scenarios.hint: Which commitment would your current routine fail first?

scenarios.title: The ledger with no bad days
scenarios.situation: Nadia keeps an attention ledger, but every entry reads the same: 'Deep minutes: 60, Interruptions: 0, Contract kept.' Her scenario accuracy is falling and her flashcards are piling up unreviewed. A friend who studied with her mentions she checked her phone 'at least five times' in their last session.
scenarios.prompt: What is broken, and what is the fix?
evidence: 14 entries, all identical: 60 deep minutes, 0 interruptions, contract kept.
choices: Her ledger is fiction — she is logging the session she wishes she had, not the one she had; the fix is immediate honest logging including every interruption, because a dishonest ledger cannot diagnose the real leak (her review system is collapsing).
Her ledger format is wrong — she needs more columns.
She needs longer sessions — 60 minutes is insufficient.
The ledger is fine — the problem is she needs a better flashcard app.
scenarios.why: An ideal student's: identical perfect entries for two weeks are statistically implausible, and the friend's observation plus the collapsing review system contradict the log. The protocol's rule is log immediately and honestly — including failures — because only true data can drive fixes. Choice 2 tweaks format when the problem is honesty. Choice 3 prescribes more time when the problem is measurement. Choice 4 blames tools for a data-integrity failure.
scenarios.hint: Whose session is the ledger describing — hers, or an ideal student's?

scenarios.title: Blocked review feels better
scenarios.situation: After the Layer 3 lesson, Tomas tries one interleaved review session (mixed domains, shuffled). It feels awful — slow, effortful, full of errors. His usual blocked sessions (one domain at a time) feel smooth and confident. He concludes interleaving 'doesn't work for him' and goes back to blocking.
scenarios.prompt: What should Tomas conclude?
choices: The feeling is the mechanism — interleaving felt harder because it forced discrimination practice (choosing which tool to use), and the delayed mock proves it worked better; he should keep interleaving and judge by delayed results, not by session comfort.
He was right — the 84% vs 58% session gap proves blocking is superior for him.
He should interleave only easy domains and block the hard ones.
The mock difference is noise — ten days is too long for the comparison to mean anything.
scenarios.why: The delayed mock: interleaving's difficulty during practice is desirable difficulty, and the 76% vs 61% delayed gap is exactly what the research predicts. Judging a technique by how smooth practice feels is the fluency trap. Choice 2 mistakes immediate performance for learning — the classic error. Choice 3 invents a compromise the evidence does not support. Choice 4 dismisses the only measurement that matters: delayed retrieval.
scenarios.hint: Which number predicts exam day — session comfort or the delayed mock?
objectives: Distinguish feeling of learning from actual learning

domains.name: Lesson Sequences
domains.summary: The lesson layer under every learning path: how ordered lesson sequences structure learning across tracks — sequencing pedagogy, dependency chains, gates, capstones, and building your own sequences.

scenarios.title: Order the Modules
scenarios.situation: You're assembling a study sequence on container orchestration. The candidate modules are: 'Deploy your first pod,' 'Kubernetes architecture: control plane and nodes,' 'Services and networking,' 'What is a container?' A colleague suggests alphabetical order.
scenarios.prompt: What ordering does sequencing pedagogy demand?
choices: Dependency order: 'What is a container?' → 'Kubernetes architecture' → 'Deploy your first pod' → 'Services and networking.' Each module's prerequisites must be satisfied by earlier modules; alphabetical order strands the learner at module one.
Alphabetical — it's the only neutral ordering.
Hardest first, to filter out unserious learners.
Random order — self-paced learners can jump anywhere anyway.
scenarios.why: A lesson sequence is an ordered progression where each step's prerequisites are met by earlier steps. The sequence layer sits under every learning path on the site for exactly this reason: order is pedagogy. Alphabetical, chronological-by-publication, or difficulty-shuffled orderings all break the dependency chain the learner is climbing.
scenarios.hint: Which module can the learner not understand without the one before it?

scenarios.title: The Cramming Sequence
scenarios.situation: A learner plans to 'complete' a 12-module sequence on networking in one weekend: 12 modules, 12 hours of video-speed reading, no labs, no self-checks, straight through.
scenarios.prompt: What breaks, pedagogically?
choices: Everything the sequence is for: one module per deep session is the rhythm — each module needs unbroken time, a lab, and self-checks before the next builds on it. Twelve modules in a weekend produces exposure, not the dependency chain the sequence promises. Slow, artifact-producing pacing is the design, not a suggestion.
Nothing — finishing fast shows motivation.
Only the labs break; the reading still counts as completion.
The weekend is too short; two weekends would fix it.
scenarios.why: Sequences are self-paced but not pace-free: the site's study rhythm is one module, one deep session, with labs and self-checks as the gates between steps. Cramming collapses the gates. Depth metrics decide completion — artifacts produced, not hours logged or modules clicked.
scenarios.hint: What will the learner have produced by Sunday night?

scenarios.title: Where Does the Capstone Go?
scenarios.situation: You're finalizing a sequence on applied cryptography. Modules cover: symmetric crypto, hashes, public-key, TLS, and a capstone project (audit a small system's crypto usage). A reviewer suggests putting the capstone second 'to motivate learners early.'
scenarios.prompt: Where does the capstone belong, and why?
choices: Last. A capstone synthesizes the whole dependency chain — it is the proof the sequence worked. Placing it early turns it into a teaser that the learner cannot yet do; the motivation it provides is frustration, not momentum. Early modules motivate through small, completable wins instead.
Second — early motivation outweighs pedagogy.
It doesn't matter; self-paced learners skip around anyway.
Split it across every module as micro-capstones with no final synthesis.
scenarios.why: Sequencing pedagogy distinguishes synthesis from motivation. Early modules earn momentum through completable labs and self-checks; the capstone earns its position at the end as the integrative artifact. A sequence that never synthesizes is a playlist, not a curriculum.
scenarios.hint: What can the learner only do after the *last* module that they couldn't do after the second?

scenarios.title: The Missing Prerequisite
scenarios.situation: Learners keep stalling at module 7 of your systems-programming sequence ('Write a minimal allocator'). Forum posts show they never actually learned pointer arithmetic — module 3 ('Memory and pointers') was marked 'optional background.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the sequencing fix?
choices: Promote the prerequisite into the chain: make module 3 required, add a self-check gate proving pointer fluency, and only then unlock the allocator module. A sequence is only as strong as its weakest assumed prerequisite — 'optional background' is where dependency chains go to die.
Make module 7 easier so the prerequisite doesn't matter.
Add a forum post explaining pointers and link it from module 7.
Remove module 7; allocators are too advanced.
scenarios.why: Every module implicitly asserts 'the learner can now do X.' When that assertion is false, everything downstream is theater. The fix is structural — required module, verifiable gate — not a link or a hint. Audit sequences by testing the assertion at each step, not by reading the titles.
scenarios.hint: Which assertion did module 7 make about the learner that wasn't true?

scenarios.title: Design a New Sequence
scenarios.situation: You've been asked to design a from-scratch 8-module sequence teaching 'Terraform and Infrastructure-as-Code' to working sysadmins. No existing sequence covers it on the site.
scenarios.prompt: What does a sound design process look like?
choices: Start from the terminal artifact: what the learner builds in the capstone (e.g. a versioned, reviewed, applied multi-environment setup). Work backward through the dependency chain — HCL syntax → state → modules → remote backends → plan/apply workflow → testing → policy → the capstone. Each module gets one deep session, a lab producing an artifact, and a self-check gate; then order strictly by dependency and cut anything that serves no downstream module.
List eight interesting Terraform topics and order them by personal preference.
Record eight lectures and call it a sequence.
Copy another site's course outline module for module.
scenarios.why: Backward design from the capstone artifact is the method: the end state defines the chain, the chain defines the modules, and each module earns its place by serving a downstream step. One module, one deep session, one artifact, one gate — then ruthless cutting of anything decorative. That is how a sequence becomes a curriculum instead of a content pile.
scenarios.hint: If a module disappeared, which later module would break?

scenarios.title: Remixing Existing Sequences
scenarios.situation: A learner wants 'the fastest path to productive Kubernetes work' and proposes stitching modules from three existing sequences: Linux System Administration, Docker and Container Engineering, and Kubernetes Certified Administrator — taking 'the interesting parts' of each.
scenarios.prompt: How do you build the remix responsibly?
choices: Extract the dependency chain, not the interesting parts: map every candidate module's prerequisites, keep the full chain for each kept module (pulling prerequisites from their home sequences), order by dependency, add one integrative capstone, and verify each gate still holds. A remix is a new sequence and must be re-validated as one — cherry-picking orphans modules from the prerequisites that made them learnable.
Take the interesting parts — motivation matters more than prerequisites.
Just do all three sequences end to end; remixes are never worth it.
Take only the capstones from each sequence.
scenarios.why: Sequences compose, but only through their dependency chains. The 'interesting parts' approach is how learners end up at module 7 without module 3. The responsible remix re-derives the chain across sequence boundaries, re-hangs the gates, and ends with its own synthesis — because the lesson layer under every path only works when the order is load-bearing.
scenarios.hint: For each 'interesting' module, where do its prerequisites live?

scenarios.title: The playlist sequence
scenarios.situation: Rena builds a 'sequence' for test-taking tactics: lesson 1, lesson 2, lesson 3, lesson 4, lesson 5, then the domain scenarios. There are no artifacts between links and no gates — just content in order.
scenarios.prompt: Why did her sequence fail, and how should she redesign it?
evidence: Link 1-5: lessons. Link 6: scenarios. Artifacts required: none. Gates: none.
Finished in 4 days. Scenario accuracy: 52%. Nothing built.
choices: It was a playlist, not a sequence — no artifacts, no handoffs, no gates; redesign with artifact links (e.g., build a time-budget template after the time lesson, run a timed drill as the gate) so each link produces something verifiable.
It was too short — she should add more lessons before the scenarios.
She went too fast — four days is insufficient for five lessons.
Sequences don't work for tactics domains — only for science domains.
scenarios.why: Nothing verifiable — a chain of lessons with no artifacts is a playlist, and the 52% accuracy shows it. Real sequences chain modules into missions where each link's output feeds the next and gates check artifacts, not lesson completion. Choice 2 adds more passive content to a passive chain. Choice 3 blames pace when the design is the problem. Choice 4 invents a domain restriction that does not exist.
scenarios.hint: What does she hold at the end of her sequence?

scenarios.title: Same-modality repair
scenarios.situation: Kwame misses 5 scenarios on Leitner-box mechanics. His repair sequence: re-read the spaced-repetition lessons, re-read his notes on the lessons, then re-take the same scenarios the next day. He scores 9/10 on the re-take and declares the weak spot fixed.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong with his repair?
evidence: Re-read lessons → re-read notes → same scenarios next day: 9/10.
choices: Everything the protocol warns against: same-modality re-learning (reading what he already read), same scenarios (recognition, not retrieval), and no delay — the 9/10 measured short-term memory, and the 4/10 two weeks later proves the weak spot was never fixed.
Nothing — 9/10 is a pass; the later 4/10 is just a bad day.
He should have re-read a third time for good measure.
Leitner boxes are too advanced — he should drop the technique.
scenarios.why: Short-term familiarity with already-seen questions — not repair. The protocol requires a different modality for re-learning (teach it, work an example), fresh scenarios for re-testing, and a real delay; Kwame did the opposite on all three. Choice 2 ignores the two-week-later data. Choice 3 doubles down on the failed modality. Choice 4 abandons a core technique instead of repairing the learning.
scenarios.hint: What did the 9/10 actually measure?

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Study Protocol as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The The Deep Work Study Protocol Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that The Deep Work Study Protocol is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in The Deep Work Study Protocol?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — The Deep Work Study Protocol issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — The Deep Work Study Protocol is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is The Deep Work Study Protocol supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any The Deep Work Study Protocol failure in Study Protocol.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to The Deep Work Study Protocol
evidence: All The Deep Work Study Protocol components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

domains.name: Start Here: Your First Session
domains.description: How this bootcamp works, how to study with it, and what the assessment measures. Complete this domain first — everything else builds on it.

scenarios.title: Maya's first session
scenarios.situation: Maya opens the bootcamp with 60 days until her certification exam. She reads three lessons in a row, highlights key sentences, and closes the tab feeling productive. She has not opened the Labs tab or attempted any scenario.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most important correction to Maya's approach?
evidence: Lessons read: 3 | Scenarios attempted: 0 | Labs opened: 0 | Artifacts produced: 0
The loop is: learn it (lessons), apply it (scenarios), build it (labs). Artifacts — not hours — measure capability.
choices: She should complete the loop: after the lessons, attempt scenarios and build the lab artifacts — reading without application and artifacts is browsing, not training.
She should read faster — three lessons is too slow; the goal is to finish all lessons in the first week.
She should highlight more carefully — better highlighting produces better retention.
Her approach is fine — understanding the ideas is the whole point; labs are optional enrichment.
scenarios.why: Reading without application produces familiarity, not capability — the bootcamp's loop is learn-apply-build, and only the full loop produces artifacts. Choice 2 confuses speed with learning; the protocol explicitly paces one module per deep session. Choice 3 is the highlighting trap: highlighting feels productive but the research shows it barely moves retention. Choice 4 inverts the bootcamp's core claim: the labs are where the method becomes habit, not optional extras.
scenarios.hint: If Maya keeps only reading, what will she have to show for it at day 60?
objectives: Distinguish passive consumption from protocol practice

scenarios.title: Two learners, one technique
scenarios.situation: Devon and Priya both learn about spaced repetition. Devon reads the lesson twice and nods along. Priya reads it once, then builds a 30-card deck from her exam material and runs her first Leitner review the same evening.
scenarios.prompt: After 30 days, who is more likely to retain the material, and why?
evidence: Lesson re-reads: 4 | Cards built: 0 | Reviews run: 0
Lesson reads: 1 | Cards built: 30 | Reviews run: 5
choices: Priya — she converted the concept into a working review system the same day; retrieval practice on her own material builds durable memory while re-reading builds only fluency.
Devon — re-reading twice encodes the material more deeply than a single read plus cards.
Neither — both approaches are equivalent since they spent the same total time.
Devon — Priya's cards are busywork; real learning happens during lesson comprehension.
scenarios.why: Priya's deck and review history are durable artifacts that keep producing retrieval practice; Devon's re-reads produced only transient fluency, which the research shows decays rapidly. Choice 2 mistakes encoding effort for encoding effectiveness — re-reading is low-effort processing. Choice 3 ignores that time-on-task is not the variable that matters; the type of processing is. Choice 4 dismisses the single most evidence-backed technique in the curriculum.
scenarios.hint: Which learner has something that still exists in 30 days?
objectives: Predict who retains more after 30 days

scenarios.title: The mock assessment surprise
scenarios.situation: After finishing all domains, Leo takes the mock assessment under timed conditions and scores 58%. He is discouraged and considers postponing his exam by three months to 're-study everything.' His domain breakdown shows: memory science 88%, test tactics 41%, everything else 60-70%.
scenarios.prompt: What should Leo do next?
evidence: memory-science 88% | active-recall 72% | spaced-repetition 65% | note-systems 61% | test-taking-tactics 41% | exam-day 66%
choices: Run a targeted repair sequence on test-taking tactics — re-learn via worked examples, drill 15 scenarios, re-test after a delay — while maintaining spaced review of the other domains; 21 days is enough for a surgical fix.
Postpone the exam three months and restart the bootcamp from lesson one.
Re-study every domain equally — a 58% means everything needs work.
Take the mock again immediately — the low score was probably nerves, and a re-take will confirm it.
scenarios.why: The breakdown shows one clear weak domain (41%) against solid others — a surgical repair sequence is the protocol's answer, and 21 days suffices. Choice 2 wastes three months on a problem that needs three weeks; choice 3 ignores the diagnostic information the mock provided; choice 4 treats a diagnostic instrument as a slot machine — immediate re-takes measure short-term memory, not repair.
scenarios.hint: What does the breakdown actually say — one problem or many?
objectives: Choose targeted repair over comprehensive re-study

scenarios.title: The comfort-rep trap
scenarios.situation: Aisha's scenario accuracy is 92% in memory science but 55% in spaced repetition. Her study sessions keep drifting back to memory-science scenarios because 'it feels good to get them right.' Her exam is in five weeks.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with Aisha's session allocation?
evidence: Last 6 sessions: 5 memory-science blocks, 1 spaced-repetition block.
choices: She is spending her effort where she is already strong — the 55% domain is the leak, and every session should prioritize repair sequences for spaced repetition until it crosses the 70% rule.
Nothing — high accuracy builds confidence, which is the most important exam asset.
She should quit scenarios entirely and just re-read the spaced-repetition lessons.
She should split time evenly — fairness across domains matters more than targeting weakness.
scenarios.why: Effort has the highest return where accuracy is lowest: the 55% domain is the leak and the 70% rule demands a repair sequence there. Choice 2 mistakes confidence for competence — the exam tests the weak domain too. Choice 3 returns to the failed modality (re-reading) instead of repair sequences. Choice 4 treats all domains as equal when the data says they are not.
scenarios.hint: Where is the marginal hour most valuable — the 92% domain or the 55% one?
objectives: Recognize comfort reps vs. productive struggle

scenarios.title: The explanation skipper
scenarios.situation: Marcus answers scenarios quickly and moves on. He reads explanations only when he gets an answer wrong — and even then, only the first sentence. His accuracy has plateaued at 68% for three weeks.
scenarios.prompt: What change is most likely to break his plateau?
evidence: Explanations read: only after wrong answers, first sentence only. Correct answers: never reviewed.
choices: Read the full explanation after every answer — including correct ones — and write the explanation's core claim in his own words; right answers for wrong reasons are future wrong answers.
Answer faster — speed builds the fluency the exam rewards.
Stop using hints — hints are making him dependent.
Switch to a different bootcamp — this one has stopped working for him.
scenarios.why: Both: he skims wrong-answer explanations and never examines correct ones, so neither outcome teaches him. The protocol requires the full explanation after every answer plus restatement in his own words — that restatement is itself retrieval practice. Choice 2 confuses speed with mastery. Choice 3 misdiagnoses: hints model reasoning moves; the problem is explanation depth, not hint use. Choice 4 blames the instrument for a user habit.
scenarios.hint: What is Marcus not learning from — his correct answers or his wrong ones?

scenarios.title: No target, no protocol
scenarios.situation: Jordan is working through the bootcamp 'to become a better learner in general.' He has no exam date, no course, and no specific material. His flashcards are generic ('What is spaced repetition?') and his labs feel abstract.
scenarios.prompt: What is the root problem, and what fixes it?
evidence: Q: What is spaced repetition? A: Reviewing at expanding intervals. Q: What is the testing effect? A: Retrieval strengthens memory.
Session audit completed — but with no real study sessions to audit, he audited his bootcamp sessions.
choices: He has no real target — the protocol runs on material you genuinely need to learn; he should pick a certification, course, or exam with a date, and rebuild his cards and labs around its actual content.
His cards need better formatting — generic cards are fine once the formatting is polished.
He should do more labs — volume of practice compensates for lack of a target.
The bootcamp is wrong for him — it only works for certification exams.
scenarios.why: Nothing real — without a target, his cards test definitions of the method instead of applying the method to content, and his labs audit bootcamp sessions instead of real study. The protocol is a machine that needs material to process. Choice 2 polishes cards that test the wrong thing. Choice 3 adds volume to a vacuum. Choice 4 is false — the method works for any real learning target, but it needs one.
scenarios.hint: What is his study material actually about?
objectives: Connect the protocol to a real target

domains.name: Memory Science: How Learning Sticks
domains.description: Encoding, the forgetting curve, sleep consolidation, chunking, and desirable difficulties — the cognitive machinery underneath every technique.

scenarios.title: The divided-attention lecture
scenarios.situation: Sam watches recorded lectures at 2x speed while answering messages. After four hours he has 'covered' six modules but cannot recall the key point of any of them. He concludes he needs to watch them again at normal speed.
scenarios.prompt: What is Sam's actual problem, and what fixes it?
evidence: 4 hours, 6 modules, 2x speed, messages throughout. Recall test: 1/12 key points.
Encoding requires focused attention; divided attention produces traces too weak to retrieve.
choices: Divided attention destroyed encoding — re-watching at normal speed with messages still on repeats the failure; the fix is single-tasking with the device rules (notifications off, phone away) plus elaborative processing per concept.
The speed — 2x is too fast; normal speed with messages on will fix it.
He needs better lectures — the material is the problem.
Four hours is too long — he should study in 10-minute bursts.
scenarios.why: Split — and encoding under divided attention fails regardless of playback speed. Re-watching at 1x with messages on is the same failure slower. Choice 3 blames content for an attention problem. Choice 4 invents a fix the evidence does not support — the issue is not session length, it is that attention was never on the material.
scenarios.hint: What was his attention doing during those four hours?

scenarios.title: Highlighting everything
scenarios.situation: Elena highlights 80% of her textbook in yellow, then re-reads the highlighted passages the night before the exam. During the exam she recognizes every question's topic but cannot produce the answers.
scenarios.prompt: Why did her method fail?
evidence: Highlight coverage: ~80% of text. Review: re-read highlights.
'I knew I had seen all of this' — score 54%.
choices: Highlighting is shallow processing — it marks surface features without semantic engagement, and re-reading builds recognition (familiarity) while the exam tests recall; she never practiced retrieving anything.
She highlighted too much — highlighting only 20% would have worked.
She should have used a pink highlighter — color matters for memory.
The exam was unfair — recognition should count as knowledge.
scenarios.why: Recall — producing answers from memory. Her entire system trained recognition: seeing marked text and feeling familiar. Familiarity masquerades as knowledge until the exam demands production. Choice 2 keeps the failed technique and tweaks the dosage. Choice 3 is superstition. Choice 4 rejects the measurement instead of fixing the method.
scenarios.hint: What did the exam ask for that her method never practiced?

scenarios.title: The missing 24-hour review
scenarios.situation: On Monday, Chris learns 40 key terms deeply — elaborative encoding, examples, full attention. He feels confident. His next review is the following Monday, seven days later, by re-reading his notes. On exam day (day 14), he recalls fewer than half.
scenarios.prompt: What single change would most improve his retention?
evidence: Day 1: deep learning. Day 7: re-read notes. Day 14: exam.
Without review, ~half is gone in a day; re-reading resets familiarity, not the curve.
choices: A retrieval attempt within 24 hours of learning — blank-page recall of the 40 terms on Tuesday, before any re-reading — which flattens the forgetting curve at its steepest point.
More elaborative encoding on Monday — he clearly did not learn them deeply enough.
Re-reading twice on day 7 instead of once.
Learning 80 terms on Monday instead of 40 — more exposure.
scenarios.why: In the first 24 hours — that is where intervention pays most, and only retrieval (not re-reading) flattens it. Chris's encoding was fine; his schedule abandoned the trace during the critical window. Choice 2 misdiagnoses an encoding problem when the evidence shows a review-timing problem. Choices 3 and 4 add volume to a mistimed system.
scenarios.hint: Where is the forgetting curve steepest?

scenarios.title: The all-nighter before the final
scenarios.situation: With 36 hours until her final, Dana decides to study through the night: 12 straight hours, energy drinks, no sleep. 'I'll sleep after the exam,' she says. She has 200 flashcards to get through.
scenarios.prompt: What should she do instead?
evidence: 12 hours overnight, 0 sleep, high caffeine. 200 cards to cover.
Sleep deprivation impairs next-day encoding ~30% and blocks consolidation; stimulants mask fatigue without restoring memory function.
choices: Study until a fixed end-time that protects 7-8 hours of sleep, run retrieval on the highest-yield cards, then sleep — consolidated partial knowledge beats unconsolidated familiarity, and she will encode tomorrow's review far better rested.
Push through — 12 hours of exposure beats 6 hours; sleep is for after the exam.
Double the energy drinks — the problem is alertness, not sleep.
Skip studying entirely and just sleep — rest beats preparation.
scenarios.why: Two things: tonight's consolidation (the studied material never gets filed) and tomorrow's encoding (the tired brain attends poorly). It is a loan with terrible terms. Choice 2 counts exposure hours while ignoring that exhausted encoding barely registers. Choice 3 treats a memory problem as an alertness problem. Choice 4 overcorrects — the protocol says protect sleep AND study hard during waking hours.
scenarios.hint: What does the all-nighter borrow against?

scenarios.title: Details without a skeleton
scenarios.situation: Omar memorizes 150 isolated facts about networking — port numbers, acronyms, defaults — with flashcards. On scenario questions that ask him to troubleshoot, he freezes: he knows the facts but cannot assemble them into reasoning.
scenarios.prompt: What is missing, and how does he build it?
evidence: Troubleshooting scenarios: 35%. 'I know the pieces but can't put them together.'
choices: Schemas — he learned details before the framework, so facts have nothing to hang on; he should build one-sentence skeletons per topic (e.g., 'TCP = reliable stream via sequence/ACK/retransmit') and re-encode each fact as attached to its skeleton, then practice explain-backs.
More facts — 150 is not enough for troubleshooting.
Faster recall — his 88% fact recall is too slow for scenarios.
Different facts — he memorized the wrong ones.
scenarios.why: Because unchunked facts are not organized knowledge — experts reason via schemas, and Omar never built them. Details-first learning scatters; skeleton-first learning assembles. Choice 2 adds more disconnected facts to the pile. Choice 3 mistakes speed for structure. Choice 4 blames content selection when the architecture is the problem.
scenarios.hint: Why can he recall facts but not reason with them?

scenarios.title: Too smooth to be true
scenarios.situation: Grace's study sessions feel wonderful: she re-reads her beautiful notes, everything looks familiar, she finishes feeling confident. Her practice exam scores: 52%, 49%, 55% across three weeks. She cannot understand the gap between how prepared she feels and how she scores.
scenarios.prompt: What explains the gap, and what changes it?
evidence: Re-reading notes, high familiarity, high confidence.
Fluent processing feels like learning but predicts recognition, not recall.
choices: Fluency illusion — re-reading produces familiarity she mistakes for mastery; the fix is desirable difficulty: closed-book retrieval, spaced reviews, interleaved scenarios, judged by delayed test scores instead of session comfort.
Test anxiety — she knows the material but chokes; she needs relaxation techniques.
Bad practice exams — they do not reflect her true knowledge.
She needs to re-read more slowly and carefully.
scenarios.why: Processing fluency — how easily the material flows past her eyes — which predicts recognition, not the recall the exam demands. Three flat practice scores are the delayed test telling the truth. Choice 2 invents anxiety the evidence does not show. Choice 3 rejects the instrument. Choice 4 prescribes more of the failed technique, slower.
scenarios.hint: What is her confidence actually measuring?

scenarios.title: Friction overload
scenarios.situation: Excited by the desirable-difficulties lesson, Theo redesigns everything at once: brand-new material learned via pure discovery with no guidance, reviews delayed 30 days, scenarios attempted before any lesson. After two weeks he has learned almost nothing and is demoralized.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong?
evidence: Discovery-only new material, 30-day delays, scenarios before lessons.
Difficulty is desirable only if the learner can overcome it; impossible difficulty is just difficulty.
choices: He applied difficulties to unlearned material at impossible levels — desirable difficulties assume initial learning has happened and must be surmountable; he should restore guided initial learning, shorten intervals to days not weeks, and add friction progressively as schemas build.
Desirable difficulties are a myth — he proved they do not work.
He did not push hard enough — 22% means he needs even longer delays.
He should switch subjects — this one is too hard for him.
scenarios.why: Two conditions: it engages the right processes and the learner can overcome it. Theo violated both — discovery-without-guidance on new material and 30-day delays are not surmountable, so they produced failure, not learning. Choice 2 generalizes from a misapplication. Choice 3 increases the poison. Choice 4 blames the subject for a calibration error.
scenarios.hint: What makes a difficulty 'desirable' versus just difficult?

domains.name: Active Recall: Retrieval Practice
domains.description: The testing effect in practice: free recall, self-quizzing, explain-backs, and flashcard craft that make retrieval the engine of learning.

scenarios.title: The re-reader's plateau
scenarios.situation: Hana studies 90 minutes daily by re-reading her notes and slides. She feels she 'knows' the material — it all looks familiar. Her practice scores have been stuck at 60% for a month. She is considering buying a second study guide.
scenarios.prompt: What is her problem and the fix?
evidence: 90 min/day re-reading. Familiarity: high. Practice scores: 60% flat for 4 weeks.
Retrieval strengthens memory far more than re-study; re-reading builds recognition, exams test recall.
choices: Her method trains recognition, not recall — the fix is replacing re-reading with daily closed-book retrieval: end each session with a 10-minute self-quiz and blank-page recall, always followed by feedback against the source.
She needs the second study guide — more material exposure will break the plateau.
She should re-read more slowly — speed is the issue.
90 minutes is not enough — she needs three hours daily.
scenarios.why: Recognition — the feeling of familiarity — which is why practice scores (recall tests) never moved. The testing effect says retrieval causes learning; her system contains zero retrieval. Choice 2 buys more content for a method problem. Choice 3 slows the same failed technique. Choice 4 adds hours to a broken process.
scenarios.hint: What has a month of re-reading actually trained?

scenarios.title: The failed retrieval
scenarios.situation: During a self-quiz, Ivan tries to explain subnetting from memory and fails completely — blank. Embarrassed, he looks up the answer, reads it carefully, and moves on. The next day he tries again and explains it cleanly.
scenarios.prompt: Was the failed attempt wasted time?
evidence: Blank — complete failure, then checked source.
choices: No — the failed attempt primed his brain to encode the feedback deeply; unsuccessful retrieval followed by checking the source beats re-study, and the next-day clean recall proves the trace was built by the attempt-plus-feedback cycle.
Yes — he should have checked the source first instead of embarrassing himself.
Yes — blank attempts mean the material is too hard; he should drop subnetting for now.
No — but only because he got lucky; failed retrievals usually encode the failure.
scenarios.why: Made it stick — effortful (even failed) retrieval primes deep encoding of the subsequent feedback; that is the mechanism behind the next-day clean recall. Choice 2 inverts the protocol: checking first converts retrieval into recognition. Choice 3 treats a productive struggle as a stop sign. Choice 4 misstates the science — failed retrieval plus feedback is one of the most robust effects in the literature.
scenarios.hint: What did the failure do to the feedback that followed?

scenarios.title: Recognition in disguise
scenarios.situation: Julia 'self-quizzes' with her old practice tests: she reads each question, glances at the choices, and picks the one that 'looks right.' She scores 85% on repeats. On the real exam — all new questions — she scores 61%.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong?
evidence: Repeated old tests, choice-recognition. Repeat score: 85%.
choices: Her practice trained recognition of seen questions, not retrieval of knowledge — she needs free-recall practice (blank-page, explain-backs, production-prompt flashcards) on the underlying concepts so new questions are answerable from understanding, not familiarity.
She needed more repeats — 85% was not high enough.
The real exam was unfair — it should reuse practice questions.
She should memorize the practice test answers — that is what they are for.
scenarios.why: Familiarity with those specific questions — a recognition score, not a knowledge score. New questions stripped the cues and exposed the gap. Choice 2 prescribes more of the failed practice. Choice 3 blames the exam for testing transfer, which is its job. Choice 4 confuses memorizing answers with learning the domain.
scenarios.hint: What did 85% actually measure?

scenarios.title: The un-scored blank page
scenarios.situation: After each session, Kevin closes his book and writes what he remembers — then closes the notebook without checking. 'The writing is the learning,' he says. His distortions go uncorrected for weeks.
scenarios.prompt: What is missing from his otherwise good habit?
evidence: Blank-page writes: daily. Source checks: never.
Confident explanations of concepts that are subtly wrong — uncorrected for weeks.
choices: Feedback — retrieval without verification risks encoding errors confidently; he must score each recall against the source, log distortions in his error log, and re-retrieve the corrected version.
Nothing — writing is indeed the learning; checking would interrupt the flow.
He should write longer recalls — more writing equals more learning.
He should recall less often — daily is overkill.
scenarios.why: It gets stronger — retrieval strengthens whatever is retrieved, including errors. Kevin is building durable misconceptions. The protocol's loop is retrieve-then-verify, never retrieve-and-hope. Choice 2 defends a habit that manufactures confident wrongness. Choice 3 adds volume to unverified output. Choice 4 reduces the frequency of the only part that works.
scenarios.hint: What happens to an uncorrected distortion after weeks of retrieval?

scenarios.title: Waiting until ready
scenarios.situation: Lena refuses to self-quiz until she 'feels ready' — she wants one more read-through first. The read-through never feels sufficient, so the quiz keeps getting postponed. Exam in 10 days; she has never attempted a closed-book recall.
scenarios.prompt: What should she do today?
evidence: 'One more read, then I'll quiz.' Quizzes attempted: 0. Days left: 10.
Testing is a cause of learning, not just a measurement — waiting until ready wastes the testing effect.
choices: Quiz immediately, closed-book, expecting failure — the failed retrievals plus feedback will build more in 10 days than another read-through; readiness is a feeling, retrieval is a mechanism.
Do the read-through first as planned — quizzing unprepared is demoralizing.
Postpone the exam — 10 days is not enough without readiness.
Quiz with notes open — a gentler start.
scenarios.why: Fluency — the comfort of recognition — which never arrives from re-reading because re-reading cannot produce it reliably. Meanwhile every postponed quiz is a lost testing-effect rep. Choice 2 protects feelings at the cost of learning. Choice 3 surrenders the exam to a mood. Choice 4 keeps the book open, which converts retrieval back into recognition.
scenarios.hint: What is 'feeling ready' actually waiting for?

scenarios.title: The stumble ignored
scenarios.situation: During an explain-back on VPN tunneling, Marco hand-waves past how the handshake authenticates — 'you know, the crypto stuff happens' — and finishes smoothly. He feels good about the session and does not log the stumble.
scenarios.prompt: What did he lose by not logging the stumble?
evidence: Smooth overall; one hand-waved gap: handshake authentication.
Exam question on handshake authentication: wrong.
choices: The diagnosis — the hand-wave marked the exact gap, and logging it would have created a retrieval target; unlogged, the gap stayed invisible until the exam found it. Explain-backs are diagnostics that talk; ignoring the stumble wastes the instrument.
Nothing — one gap in a smooth explanation is normal.
Time — logging stumbles takes too long for the value.
Confidence — logging gaps would have hurt his morale before the exam.
scenarios.why: A precise gap detector firing — 'the crypto stuff happens' is the audible signature of missing knowledge. The protocol says every stumble becomes a retrieval target; Marco's smooth feeling was fluency about the parts he knew, masking the part he did not. Choices 2-4 all rationalize ignoring the single most informative moment of the session.
scenarios.hint: What was the hand-wave, functionally?

scenarios.title: The essay card pile
scenarios.situation: Nadia has 400 flashcards. A typical card: 'Explain the OSI model.' She flips through them, reading the backs when stuck, and calls it review. Sessions take 90 minutes; retention is poor; she dreads the deck.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with her deck, and what is the fix?
evidence: 400 cards, essay prompts ('Explain X'), backs read when stuck.
choices: The cards are essays, not retrievals — 'Explain the OSI model' is a reading assignment that gets skimmed, and reading backs when stuck is recognition; she should split cards to atomic one-fact prompts ('What does the transport layer guarantee?'), use production prompts, and suspend cards she always gets right.
She needs more cards — 400 is insufficient coverage.
She should read the backs first — it is more efficient.
Flashcards do not work for her — she should switch to re-reading.
scenarios.why: Giving up — the retrieval attempt is aborted at the first difficulty, so the testing effect never fires, and the back-read builds recognition. Atomic cards make each retrieval clean, quick, and gradable; her essay cards make honest retrieval nearly impossible. Choice 2 adds cards to a broken format. Choice 3 makes it worse. Choice 4 abandons the technique instead of fixing the craft.
scenarios.hint: What does flipping to the back 'when stuck' actually practice?

domains.name: Spaced Repetition: Timing Your Reviews
domains.description: Spacing intervals, the Leitner box system, review triage, and deciding what deserves spacing versus what deserves drilling.

scenarios.title: The weekly cram review
scenarios.situation: Paula reviews all 300 of her flashcards every Sunday in one 3-hour session. By Wednesday she has forgotten most of them again. 'I just reviewed them!' she says.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with her schedule?
evidence: Sunday: all 300 cards, 3 hours. Wed–Sat: nothing.
Wednesday recall: poor. 'I just reviewed them!'
choices: Massed weekly review ignores the forgetting curve — 7-day gaps let traces decay fully between sessions, and reviewing all cards uniformly wastes reps on strong cards while starving weak ones; she needs per-card expanding intervals with the critical day-one review.
300 cards is too many — she should delete half.
Sunday is the wrong day — reviews work better on Tuesdays.
3 hours is too long — she should review for 30 minutes.
scenarios.why: It decays — the forgetting curve does not pause because a review is scheduled next week. Paula re-learns every Sunday instead of retrieving, because the interval exceeds what her traces survive. Choice 2 blames quantity when timing is the problem. Choice 3 is superstition about weekdays. Choice 4 shortens the same mistimed session.
scenarios.hint: What happens to a memory trace between Sunday and the next Sunday?
objectives: Replace massed review with spaced retrieval

scenarios.title: The dishonest grader
scenarios.situation: Tom uses a spaced-repetition app and grades every recall 'easy' to get through reviews faster. His intervals stretch to 30+ days. At each review he blanks on most cards and has to re-learn them.
scenarios.prompt: What is his grading doing to his intervals?
evidence: 'Easy' on 95% of cards, including struggled recalls.
30+ days. Review outcome: mostly blanks, re-learning.
choices: Lying to the scheduler — 'easy' promises the algorithm he will remember in 30 days, but the promise is false, so every review arrives past the forgetting edge and becomes re-learning; honest grading ('hard' for struggles, 'again' for failures) keeps intervals inside retrievability.
Nothing — the algorithm corrects for dishonest grading automatically.
Speeding up learning — faster reviews mean more reps.
The app is broken — intervals should never reach 30 days.
scenarios.why: A prediction about future retrievability that sets the next interval. Tom's 'easy' grades are false predictions, so the scheduler spaces reviews beyond his actual retention. Choice 2 invents a correction mechanism that does not exist. Choice 3 confuses clearing the queue with learning. Choice 4 blames the tool for the user's dishonest input.
scenarios.hint: What is a grade, functionally?

scenarios.title: The avalanche
scenarios.situation: Excited, Rosa adds 150 new cards in one weekend. Her daily reviews jump from 40 to 350. After four days of 2-hour review sessions, she abandons the system entirely — 'spaced repetition doesn't work.'
scenarios.prompt: What killed her system?
choices: Uncapped additions — new cards create future review obligations, and 150 at once exceeded her daily capacity; the fix is adding in batches sized to a completable daily load (e.g., 10-20/day) so the system survives bad days.
Spaced repetition — the technique genuinely does not scale.
Her willpower — she should have pushed through the 2-hour sessions.
The cards — 150 was the wrong content.
scenarios.why: Future reviews — a card is a recurring obligation, not a one-time task. Rosa bought 150 obligations in a weekend against a 40-review budget. The protocol's rule: new cards per day ≤ what you can review on your worst day. Choice 2 blames the technique for a capacity error. Choice 3 prescribes unsustainable heroics. Choice 4 blames content for arithmetic.
scenarios.hint: What does each new card actually cost?
objectives: Cap new cards by review capacity

scenarios.title: The untouchable leech
scenarios.situation: One card — 'Explain the differences between symmetric and asymmetric encryption, including key exchange, performance, and use cases' — has failed 11 times. Each failure, David just hits 'again' and moves on. It has consumed 40+ reviews.
scenarios.prompt: What should David do with this card?
evidence: Failed 11 times. Reviews consumed: 40+. Action taken: none.
'Explain the differences between symmetric and asymmetric encryption, including key exchange, performance, and use cases'
choices: Operate: it is five cards wearing a trench coat — split into atomic cards (one per sub-question: key exchange, performance, use cases, key count, examples), rewrite prompts as production questions, add a concrete example to each; never just keep failing it.
Keep hitting 'again' — persistence will eventually work.
Delete it — encryption is not that important.
Memorize the back verbatim — recitation will fix it.
scenarios.why: It is unanswerable as written — a multi-part essay prompt that cannot be cleanly retrieved or graded, so every attempt is partial and every failure teaches nothing. Leech surgery (split, rewrite, exemplify) addresses the cause; repetition addresses nothing. Choice 2 is the definition of grinding. Choice 3 abandons examinable content. Choice 4 builds recitation, not understanding.
scenarios.hint: Why does this card keep failing?

scenarios.title: Spacing the skill
scenarios.situation: Mei puts subnetting practice into her spaced deck: one subnetting problem card reviewed on expanding intervals (day 1, 3, 7, 14...). Between reviews she does no other subnetting practice. Her calculation speed never improves.
scenarios.prompt: What is mismatched?
evidence: Subnetting as spaced cards, expanding intervals, no between-session practice.
Accuracy okay, speed stagnant. 'I can do it but too slowly for the exam.'
choices: The practice type — subnetting is a skill, and skills need concentrated drill blocks with varied problems and feedback, not just spaced single reps; she should drill in focused sessions and use spacing only for maintenance.
The intervals — they should be shorter.
The cards — she needs more subnetting cards.
Subnetting — it cannot be learned with flashcards at all.
scenarios.why: Concentrated varied reps with feedback — the drill block. Spacing maintains declarative knowledge; it cannot build procedural fluency one rep per week. Mei spaced a skill that needed drilling. Choice 2 tweaks timing when the modality is wrong. Choice 3 adds cards to the wrong practice type. Choice 4 overcorrects — the content is fine, the method assignment is wrong.
scenarios.hint: What builds speed at a procedural skill?
objectives: Match practice type to knowledge type

scenarios.title: The comfort reps
scenarios.situation: Leo's daily review: he spends 25 minutes on box-5 cards he always gets right ('warming up') and rushes through box-1 cards in 5 minutes. Box 1 keeps growing. He feels productive every day.
scenarios.prompt: Where is his effort misallocated?
evidence: 25 min: box-5 cards, 100% correct. 5 min: box-1 cards, rushed.
choices: Inverted — box-5 cards need the least attention (they are durable) and box-1 the most (they are the leak); he should triage box 1 first with full effort and let strong cards take their long intervals undisturbed.
Nowhere — warming up on easy cards is good practice.
He needs more total time — 30 minutes is insufficient.
Box 1 is growing because the system is broken — he should reset it.
scenarios.why: Consuming 80% of his effort on cards that need ~0% of it — comfort reps that feel productive while the real work (box 1) starves. The Leitner system's whole point is automatic triage toward weakness; Leo manually overrides it toward comfort. Choice 2 defends the inversion. Choice 3 adds time to a misallocation. Choice 4 blames the system for the user's prioritization.
scenarios.hint: What is the 'warm-up' actually doing?

scenarios.title: The skipped day-one
scenarios.situation: On Monday, Ana learns 25 new concepts with excellent encoding. 'I'll start the spaced reviews next Monday when I do my weekly review.' By next Monday, she retrieves 6 of 25.
scenarios.prompt: What single change fixes this?
evidence: Monday: learn. Next review: following Monday (7 days).
choices: A day-one retrieval session — 15 minutes of blank-page recall on Tuesday before any re-reading; the first interval is the highest-leverage review because the forgetting curve is steepest in the first 24 hours.
Better encoding on Monday — 25 concepts was too many.
Reviewing twice on the following Monday instead of once.
Learning fewer concepts — 25 is too ambitious.
scenarios.why: They decayed past retrieval during the curve's steepest window — no review intervened, so by day 7 Ana was re-learning, not reviewing. One 15-minute day-one retrieval would have flattened the curve for most of them. Choice 2 misdiagnoses encoding when the schedule is the failure. Choice 3 doubles a too-late review. Choice 4 reduces ambition instead of fixing timing.
scenarios.hint: What happened to the 19 lost concepts between Monday and Monday?
objectives: Apply the forgetting curve's steepest point

domains.name: Note Systems: Building a Second Brain
domains.description: Atomic linked notes, question-based notes, modern Cornell, and the weekly synthesis that turns notes into durable artifacts.

scenarios.title: The stenographer
scenarios.situation: During lectures, Priya types everything the instructor says, verbatim — 40 pages per course. She never re-reads them. Before the exam she skims the 40 pages once. Score: 57%.
scenarios.prompt: Why did 40 pages of notes produce a 57%?
evidence: 40 pages, verbatim transcription. Re-reads: 0 (one skim pre-exam).
Notes could have been produced by a stenographer with zero understanding.
choices: Transcription bypasses semantic processing — her brain was a keyboard, not a learner — and write-only notes are never revisited, so the hours bought nothing; she needs atomic thinking-notes in her own words, linked, with scheduled retrieval reviews.
She typed too slowly — handwriting is better for memory.
40 pages is too many — she should transcribe less.
She skimmed instead of reading carefully — the skim was the problem.
scenarios.why: Keystrokes — not meaning. Copying verbatim requires no understanding, so no understanding was encoded; and unreviewed notes are an archive, not a study tool. Choice 2 debates input devices while the processing is the problem. Choice 3 keeps transcription and reduces it. Choice 4 blames the skim when the notes were never learnable from.
scenarios.hint: What did the act of typing actually process?

scenarios.title: The unlinked pile
scenarios.situation: Devon has 2,000 digital notes collected over a year — highlights, clippings, summaries. When he needs the insight about spacing intervals for his exam prep, he cannot find it. Search returns 300 matches.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with his collection?
evidence: Cannot locate the specific insight when needed.
choices: It is a landfill, not a system — unlinked chronological notes are unfindable, and unreviewed clippings were never processed; he needs atomic notes with claim-titles, real links between ideas, and scheduled revisits so the network retrieves itself.
He needs a better search engine.
2,000 notes is too many — he should delete most.
Digital notes are the problem — paper would fix it.
scenarios.why: Because his notes lack the structure search needs: claim-titles, links, and his own processing. 300 matches for 'spacing' means none of them is findable as the idea he needs. Choice 2 upgrades the tool for a structure problem. Choice 3 deletes the archive instead of organizing it. Choice 4 changes the medium, not the method.
scenarios.hint: Why does search fail him?

scenarios.title: Questions asked too late
scenarios.situation: After reading a chapter, Sofia writes excellent question-notes — thoughtful why/how questions with good answers. But she writes them with the book open, copying adapted phrasing, and never re-quizzes them.
scenarios.prompt: What two fixes does she need?
evidence: Excellent, exam-mirroring. Written with book open.
0. The notes sit in a folder.
choices: Close the book before writing answers (open-book answers are transcription with extra steps) and schedule cover-and-retrieve reviews of the questions — a question never re-answered is just a note with punctuation.
Better questions — hers are not good enough.
More questions — quantity is the issue.
Handwritten questions — digital does not work.
scenarios.why: Transcription — the retrieval never happens because the answer is visible during writing. And without re-quizzing, even genuine questions decay into statements. Sofia is one habit (close the book) and one schedule (re-quiz) away from a self-testing system. Choices 2-4 fiddle with everything except the two actual failures.
scenarios.hint: What is an open-book 'answer' actually?

scenarios.title: The summary-first synthesis
scenarios.situation: Each week, Marco 'synthesizes' by re-reading his notes and writing a summary of what they say. His syntheses read like condensed textbooks. His open confusions are never listed — 'I don't want to focus on the negative.'
scenarios.prompt: What is his synthesis missing?
evidence: Notes-first, condensed-textbook style. Open questions listed: 0.
Exactly the topics his syntheses glossed over.
choices: Retrieval and honesty — drafting from memory first would expose gaps (the draft-vs-notes gap is the learning edge), and unlisted confusions stay unaddressed; his notes-first summaries just repackage what he already processed.
Length — his syntheses are too short.
Formatting — they need better headings.
Frequency — weekly is not enough; he needs daily.
scenarios.why: That the synthesis contains only what the notes contain — no retrieval, no gap detection, no diagnosis. And refusing to list confusions means the curriculum never learns what to target. His exam gaps are the unlisted confusions, found too late. Choices 2-4 polish a process whose core (memory-first, confusion inventory) is absent.
scenarios.hint: What does notes-first drafting guarantee?

scenarios.title: The three-idea note
scenarios.situation: Aisha's 'atomic' notes each contain three paragraphs covering three related ideas. When she reviews, she half-remembers each idea. Her links point to whole notes, so following a link retrieves a jumble.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with her atomicity?
evidence: Title: 'Spacing.' Body: 3 paragraphs — intervals, Leitner, and review triage.
Half-recall of each idea; links land in jumbles.
choices: The notes are atomic in name only — three ideas per note means no idea is cleanly retrievable, gradable, or linkable; she must split to one idea per note with claim-titles so each unit can be recalled, tested, and linked precisely.
Nothing — related ideas belong together.
Her titles are bad — 'Spacing' is too vague.
She needs longer notes — three paragraphs is too short.
scenarios.why: Everything downstream: retrieval is partial (half of each), failures are ambiguous (which idea failed?), and links are imprecise (which idea does the link mean?). Atomicity is what makes notes combinable and testable. Choice 2 defends the jumble. Choice 3 tweaks titles while the unit is wrong. Choice 4 lengthens the problem.
scenarios.hint: What breaks when a note holds three ideas?

scenarios.title: Cues copied fresh
scenarios.situation: For his Cornell pages, Jamal fills the cue column during the lecture, copying key terms from the slides. At review time he covers the right side and 'answers' the cues — but he is just matching terms he copied an hour ago.
scenarios.prompt: Why is his Cornell review ineffective?
evidence: Written during lecture, copied from slides.
choices: The cues were never a retrieval — copied fresh from slides, they test nothing; cues must be written after the session from memory (itself a retrieval practice) and phrased as questions demanding understanding, so the cover-and-answer review is genuine.
Cornell does not work for lectures — only for reading.
He should write more cues — coverage is the issue.
The cover-and-answer step is unnecessary — reading cues is enough.
scenarios.why: Term matching from short-term memory — the cues were copied an hour earlier, so answering them retrieved nothing durable. The protocol requires cues written after, from memory, as real questions. Choice 2 invents a modality restriction. Choice 3 adds cues to a broken process. Choice 4 removes the only retrieval in the system.
scenarios.hint: What did his 'review' actually rehearse?

scenarios.title: The museum
scenarios.situation: Elena built a beautiful Zettelkasten: 300 atomic notes, claim-titles, thoughtful links. She has not opened it in two months — 'it's all in there when I need it.' Her exam is in three weeks and the network feels unfamiliar.
scenarios.prompt: What happened to her second brain?
evidence: 300 atomic linked notes. Last opened: 2 months ago.
choices: It became a museum — a network never revisited decays like any memory; notes need scheduled retrieval (question-note reviews, synthesis passes, link-walking) to stay alive, and 'stored' is not 'known.'
300 notes is too many — the system collapsed under its own weight.
Zettelkasten does not work for exams — only for research.
She needs more links — the network is too sparse.
scenarios.why: Retrieval history — Elena stored 300 notes but retrieved none for two months, so the network is unfamiliar when she needs it most. A second brain needs exercise like a first brain. Choice 2 blames scale when the issue is zero revisits. Choice 3 invents a use-case restriction. Choice 4 prescribes more structure for an unused system.
scenarios.hint: What is the difference between 'stored' and 'known'?

domains.name: Elaboration & Interleaving: Deep Processing
domains.description: Elaborative interrogation, the Feynman technique, interleaved practice, concrete examples, and dual coding for deep durable understanding.

scenarios.title: The borrowed analogy
scenarios.situation: When asked how spaced repetition works, Kevin recites the textbook's analogy: 'It's like watering plants at the right time.' Pressed on why the intervals expand rather than staying fixed, he goes blank.
scenarios.prompt: What does his blank reveal?
evidence: Textbook analogy recited fluently. Follow-up 'why expanding?': blank.
Reading someone else's analogy is recognition; inventing your own is elaboration.
choices: He never elaborated — the borrowed analogy gave him fluent words without the underlying mechanism; generating his own explanation (why expanding intervals match strengthening traces) would have built the understanding the recitation faked.
The analogy is bad — he needs a better one from a different book.
He needs to memorize the analogy harder.
Analogies do not work for him — he should stick to definitions.
scenarios.why: The textbook author's — Kevin rented the analogy without doing the cognitive work, so it came with no understanding attached. The protocol demands generative elaboration: your own why, your own example, your own analogy. Choice 2 shops for better rentals. Choice 3 memorizes harder. Choice 4 abandons the technique instead of doing it properly.
scenarios.hint: Whose elaboration was in his answer?

scenarios.title: The smooth blocked session
scenarios.situation: For her networking exam, Lisa practices 30 subnetting problems in a row (smooth, 90%), then 30 port-number recalls in a row (smooth, 95%). On the mixed exam, she scores 68% — 'the questions kept switching on me.'
scenarios.prompt: Why did blocked mastery collapse on the mixed exam?
choices: She never practiced choosing — blocked practice trains execution of a warmed-up strategy; the exam interleaves, demanding discrimination (which tool for this question?); only interleaved practice trains that choice.
She did not practice enough — 60 problems is too few.
The exam was harder than practice — the percentages do not transfer.
She should have blocked harder — more reps per block.
scenarios.why: Strategy selection under switching — the exam's questions arrive unlabeled and mixed, but her practice always announced the type by blocking. Interleaving is discrimination practice; blocking is execution practice. Choice 2 adds reps of the wrong type. Choice 3 blames difficulty for a transfer gap. Choice 4 doubles down on the failed format.
scenarios.hint: What skill did the exam test that her practice never trained?

scenarios.title: The jargon shield
scenarios.situation: Asked to explain TCP flow control simply, Omar says: 'The receiver advertises a window and the sender throttles its transmission rate to avoid buffer overflow.' Asked what a 'window' actually is, he says: 'You know, the window.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the 'you know, the window' moment telling him?
evidence: Jargon is a hiding place for partial understanding.
choices: Exactly where his understanding ends — the jargon shielded a gap, and the Feynman constraint (explain to a 12-year-old, no jargon) would force him to re-learn what a window actually is: the receiver's available buffer space, in bytes.
Nothing — everyone uses jargon; it is efficient.
He explained it fine — the questioner was being pedantic.
He needs more jargon — technical precision requires it.
scenarios.why: Hiding — 'window' and 'throttles' stood in for mechanisms he could not articulate. Fluency with terms is not understanding of mechanisms, and the Feynman technique's whole job is stripping that cover. Choice 2 normalizes the hiding. Choice 3 blames the questioner for finding the gap. Choice 4 prescribes more camouflage.
scenarios.hint: What was the jargon doing in his explanation?

scenarios.title: The single example
scenarios.situation: For 'opportunity cost,' Ana learned one example: 'attending college instead of working.' On exam questions applying the concept to business decisions, she freezes — 'we never covered business examples.'
scenarios.prompt: Why couldn't she transfer the concept?
evidence: Opportunity cost: 1 example (college vs work). Exam: business scenarios — frozen.
One example fuses with the concept; diverse examples keep the abstraction general and transferable.
choices: Single-example fusion — her one example became the concept, so new contexts did not match the pattern; two or more diverse examples (college, business investment, time allocation) keep the abstraction general and transferable.
She needed to memorize the definition harder.
Business examples are a different concept — the exam was unfair.
She should have studied business instead of economics.
scenarios.why: The college story — one example fused with the abstraction, so the concept only retrieved in that costume. Diverse examples teach the brain the principle behind the instances. Choice 2 prescribes definition-memorization for a transfer failure. Choice 3 denies that transfer is the exam's job. Choice 4 changes the subject instead of the method.
scenarios.hint: What did her brain file 'opportunity cost' under?

scenarios.title: The admired diagram
scenarios.situation: Theo printed the textbook's beautiful TCP state diagram and pinned it above his desk. He looks at it daily. Asked to sketch the connection states from memory, he cannot — 'I know it when I see it.'
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with his dual coding?
evidence: Cannot sketch from memory. 'I know it when I see it.'
choices: It is passive — admiring someone else's diagram is recognition; dual coding requires generating the visual yourself (translating words into your own sketch) and retrieving it from memory (sketching blank-page). His 'knowing' is familiarity with the image.
The diagram is too complex — he needs a simpler one.
He should look at it more often — frequency is the issue.
Diagrams do not work for him — he is a verbal learner.
scenarios.why: Recognition — the weakest form of knowing, and useless when the exam demands production. The elaborative work is in the translation (words → your diagram) and the retrieval (blank-page sketch). Choice 2 simplifies the wrong thing. Choice 3 adds admiration reps. Choice 4 invokes learning-styles mythology to excuse passive study.
scenarios.hint: What does 'I know it when I see it' actually describe?

scenarios.title: Interleaving too early
scenarios.situation: Two days into learning subnetting, Ivan mixes subnetting, supernetting, and VLSM problems randomly. He gets 20% and concludes interleaving 'doesn't work.' He had not yet understood any of the three types separately.
scenarios.prompt: What was his mistake?
evidence: Day 2 of subnetting; mixed 3 unlearned types. Score: 20%.
Interleave after initial learning — mixing incomprehension is not desirable difficulty.
choices: Timing — interleaving assumes each type is initially understood; on day 2 he had no schemas to discriminate between, so the mixing produced confusion, not discrimination practice. Block each type first, then interleave.
Interleaving is a myth — his experiment disproves it.
He needed harder problems — 20% means the problems were too easy to engage him.
He should interleave more types — three was too few.
scenarios.why: Something to discriminate between — understood schemas for each type. Ivan tried to choose between strategies he had not learned, which is not desirable difficulty (surmountable) but impossible difficulty. Choice 2 generalizes from a misapplication. Choice 3 inverts the diagnosis. Choice 4 adds confusion to confusion.
scenarios.hint: What does discrimination practice require?

scenarios.title: Decorating confusion
scenarios.situation: Sofia does not understand public-key cryptography, so she spends an hour finding the perfect analogy — 'it's like a magical mailbox!' — and drawing it beautifully. On the exam's key-exchange question, she still cannot reason about it.
scenarios.prompt: Why didn't the analogy save her?
evidence: Beautiful analogy and drawing for a concept she does not understand.
choices: Elaboration decorates understanding; it cannot substitute for it — she connected a vivid image to a hollow core, so the image retrieved nothing mechanistic. The fix is understanding first (Feynman the mechanism), elaboration second.
The analogy was wrong — a better analogy would have worked.
She needed more analogies — one was insufficient.
Drawing is a waste of time — she should have re-read.
scenarios.why: A gap — the elaboration was vivid but the underlying mechanism was missing, so the beautiful mailbox retrieved no reasoning power. The protocol's order: understand (Feynman, worked examples), then elaborate (analogies, connections). Choice 2 shops for better decorations. Choice 3 multiplies them. Choice 4 retreats to the failed technique.
scenarios.hint: What was her analogy attached to?

domains.name: Metacognition: Managing Your Own Learning
domains.description: Calibration, the plan-monitor-evaluate cycle, error logs, and defeating the illusions of competence that fake fluency creates.

scenarios.title: The 85% prediction
scenarios.situation: Before a 20-scenario block on spaced repetition, Ravi predicts 85% — 'I studied this well.' He scores 60%. 'The questions were tricky,' he says, and predicts 85% again next time.
scenarios.prompt: What is miscalibrated, and how does he fix it?
evidence: Block 1: predicted 85%, actual 60%. Block 2: predicted 85%, actual 63%.
