choices: His predictions are anchored on fluency, not tested history — re-reading feels like knowing; the fix is basing predictions on last week's actual accuracy per domain and tracking prediction-vs-actual until the gap shrinks.
His studying — 60% means he needs to study harder.
The scenarios — they are trickier than the lessons suggest.
His attitude — he needs more confidence.
scenarios.why: His feeling during re-reading — fluency — which has near-zero correlation with recall performance. Two blocks of 60-ish% are the data; the prediction should follow the data, not the feeling. Choice 2 treats the symptom. Choice 3 blames the instrument. Choice 4 prescribes the disease (more confidence) as the cure.
scenarios.hint: What is his 85% actually predicting?

scenarios.title: The drifting session
scenarios.situation: Mei plans 20 interleaved scenarios. At minute 25 she notices she has drifted into re-reading box-5 flashcards — comfortable, familiar. She thinks 'I'll get back to the plan after this deck' and continues.
scenarios.prompt: What did she do wrong at minute 25?
evidence: Drifted to box-5 comfort reps. Noticed. Continued anyway.
choices: Noticed the drift but didn't correct — monitoring without action is just narration; the mid-session tick must trigger an immediate return to the plan, because 'after this deck' never comes.
Nothing — noticing drift is the skill; she did it.
Her plan was too hard — interleaved scenarios were unrealistic.
She should plan shorter sessions — 25 minutes is her limit.
scenarios.why: Correction — monitoring is a control loop: detect, correct, verify. Mei ran open-loop: she detected and continued, so the plan died at minute 25. Choice 2 celebrates half the skill. Choice 3 blames the plan for a control failure. Choice 4 redesigns around the failure instead of fixing it.
scenarios.hint: What is the difference between noticing drift and monitoring?

scenarios.title: Answers without causes
scenarios.situation: Tom's error log has 60 entries. Each reads: 'Q12 — answer was C.' None records why he chose wrong, and he never re-tests. Before the exam he skims the log. Score: unchanged from his last mock.
scenarios.prompt: Why didn't his log help?
evidence: 'Q12 — answer was C.' 'Q31 — answer was A.' (60 entries, same format)
choices: It records answers, not causes — 'answer was C' contains no diagnosis, so no fix was ever prescribed; and without re-testing, entries never close. A bug tracker with no root causes and no verification is a worry list.
60 entries is too few — he needs more data.
He skimmed instead of studying the log deeply.
Error logs do not work — he should drop the technique.
scenarios.why: Nothing — the entry contains no information about why he missed it, so it prescribes no fix and predicts no future miss. Root-cause entries (misread? gap? trap?) are actionable; answer entries are trivia. Choice 2 wants more trivia. Choice 3 studies trivia harder. Choice 4 abandons the tool instead of using it correctly.
scenarios.hint: What can he do with 'Q12 — answer was C'?

scenarios.title: The clear lecture illusion
scenarios.situation: After a brilliant 90-minute lecture on distributed consensus, Ana feels she fully understands it. 'That was so clear!' That evening's blank-page recall: she produces 2 of 9 key points and cannot reconstruct the main argument.
scenarios.prompt: What happened?
evidence: 2/9 key points. Main argument: not reconstructable.
choices: She experienced the lecturer's understanding, not her own — clarity of teaching creates fluency in the listener, which masquerades as comprehension; only unaided production (blank-page, Feynman) tests whether the understanding transferred.
The lecture was too advanced — she needs a simpler one.
She has a bad memory — 2/9 is abnormal.
Evening recall is unfair — she was tired.
scenarios.why: The lecturer's — brilliant teaching produces fluent processing in the audience, and fluent processing feels like knowing. The blank page is the audit that feelings cannot perform. Choice 2 blames content level for a universal illusion. Choice 3 pathologizes a normal effect. Choice 4 excuses the only honest measurement she took.
scenarios.hint: Whose understanding did she feel during the lecture?

scenarios.title: Five misreadings
scenarios.situation: Reviewing his error log, David finds 5 misses this week — all the same root cause: he misread the prompt (missed 'NOT,' 'EXCEPT,' 'BEST'). He schedules 'more content review' for next week.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with his plan?
choices: It treats a systemic reading problem as five knowledge problems — the cluster says his question-parsing protocol is broken, and the fix is a reading ritual (underline negatives, restate the prompt before answering), not more content.
Nothing — more review never hurts.
He needs easier questions — the prompts are tricky.
Five is too few to matter — he should wait for more data.
scenarios.why: One systemic problem wearing five disguises — and content review cannot fix a parsing failure. Clustering exists precisely to catch this: the fix targets the process (how he reads), not the content (what he knows). Choice 2 prescribes the wrong medicine. Choice 3 blames the exam for testing careful reading. Choice 4 waits while the leak continues.
scenarios.hint: What do five identical root causes indicate?

scenarios.title: The 'I knew it' blank
scenarios.situation: On a scenario about Leitner demotion, Omar blanks completely. 'I knew that — I just blanked under pressure,' he says, and does not log it. On the next mock, he blanks on it again.
scenarios.prompt: What is the 'I knew it' story costing him?
evidence: Complete blank on demotion rule. Not logged: 'I knew it.'
choices: The diagnosis — 'I just blanked' is the fluency illusion defending itself; the blank is data (a retrieval failure needing tighter intervals and an atomic card), and unlogged it repeats. Knowing means recallable under pressure.
Nothing — everyone blanks sometimes.
His confidence — he should be kinder to himself.
Time — logging blanks takes too long.
scenarios.why: Because 'knew' meant 'recognized when cued,' not 'recallable under pressure' — and exams test the latter. The blank is the measurement; the story is the excuse. Logging it as a retrieval failure would have prescribed the fix (shorter intervals, atomic card). Choices 2-4 all protect the story instead of reading the data.
scenarios.hint: If he 'knew it,' why did it blank twice?

scenarios.title: Planning without mechanism
scenarios.situation: Lena's session plan: 'Study spaced repetition hard for 2 hours.' Afterward she cannot say whether it worked — 'I studied hard, I think it went well.' Her accuracy is flat.
scenarios.prompt: What makes her plan unusable?
choices: It states no mechanism and no target — 'study hard' cannot be evaluated, so no learning about her learning occurs; a real plan names the method ('20 interleaved scenarios'), the reason ('discrimination is my weak link'), and the target ('75%'), making the post-session evaluation possible.
Two hours is too long — she needs shorter sessions.
Her attitude is wrong — she needs to take it more seriously.
Planning is overkill — she should just study.
scenarios.why: Nothing checkable — without a mechanism and target, the session is ungradeable and the flat accuracy teaches her nothing about what to change. The M-cycle needs a plan specific enough to be wrong. Choice 2 redesigns duration for a specificity problem. Choice 3 moralizes. Choice 4 abandons the steering wheel.
scenarios.hint: What can she conclude from 'I studied hard'?

scenarios.title: The unrecorded prediction
scenarios.situation: Before each block, Marco thinks 'I'll probably get around 70%' but never writes it down. Afterward he thinks 'yeah, that feels about right' regardless of the score. His calibration never improves.
scenarios.prompt: Why isn't his calibration improving?
evidence: 'Feels about right' — at 55% and at 80% alike.
choices: Hindsight edits unrecorded predictions — memory revises the 'prediction' to match the outcome, so no error signal ever survives; written predictions before and written actuals after create an uneditable gap that forces learning.
He is bad at predicting — some people just can't calibrate.
70% is the wrong anchor — he should predict higher.
Calibration does not matter — only the score matters.
scenarios.why: It gets rewritten by hindsight — 'I knew I'd get 55%' feels true after the fact, destroying the error signal calibration needs. The written record is the only prediction that cannot be edited. Choice 2 declares the skill unlearnable; it is trainable with recorded feedback. Choice 3 tweaks the anchor. Choice 4 dismisses the steering instrument.
scenarios.hint: What happens to a prediction that was never written?

domains.name: Focus Management: Energy & Environment
domains.description: Energy over time management, environment design, session architecture, attention training, and deliberate recovery as strategy.

scenarios.title: The phone on the desk
scenarios.situation: Chris studies with his phone face-down on the desk — 'it's on silent, so it's fine.' His attention ledger shows 11 pickups per 90-minute session, averaging 4 minutes each. He insists the phone isn't the problem because 'I always get back to work.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the phone actually costing him?
evidence: 11 pickups/session, ~4 min each = 44 min. Deep minutes: ~46 of 90.
choices: Half his session — 44 minutes of pickups plus the re-focus cost after each (attention residue means the minutes around each pickup are also degraded); the fix is physical distance (phone in another room), not willpower, because willpower is consulted 11 times and loses.
Nothing — 46 deep minutes is fine.
He should get a better phone — faster pickups would save time.
Silent mode is the problem — he should turn sound on so he notices.
scenarios.why: The residue — each return carries attention residue from the phone, so the minutes after a pickup are degraded too; and 11 willpower contests per session is a design failure, not a discipline failure. Physical distance removes the contest entirely. Choice 2 accepts a 50% loss. Choice 3 optimizes the distraction. Choice 4 is absurd.
scenarios.hint: What does 'I always get back to work' ignore?

scenarios.title: The 3pm grind
scenarios.situation: Pat's energy audit shows peak focus 8-11am and a deep trough 2-4pm. She schedules her hardest topic (new concepts) for 3pm 'to get it out of the way' and does email at 9am. Her encoding is poor and she feels behind.
scenarios.prompt: What is inverted, and what is the fix?
choices: Her schedule is upside-down — prime cognitive hours go to email (shallow) while the trough gets the hardest encoding; swap them: new concepts at 8-11am, admin and light reviews in the trough.
Nothing — discipline overcomes energy dips.
She should drink coffee at 3pm — the trough is fixable with caffeine.
Her audit is wrong — energy does not affect learning.
scenarios.why: Email — the lowest-cognitive-value task in her day. Meanwhile her hardest encoding lands in the trough, where the depleted brain barely registers it. Same hours, swapped allocation, ~15% accuracy gains in the research pattern. Choice 2 denies the data. Choice 3 borrows energy at interest. Choice 4 denies the premise the audit proved.
scenarios.hint: What is she spending her peak hours on?

scenarios.title: The heroic jump
scenarios.situation: Sam's current max is 20 unbroken minutes. Inspired, he sets a target of 2-hour deep blocks. Day 1: collapses at 35 minutes, feels like a failure. Day 3: stops trying — 'I just can't focus.'
scenarios.prompt: What should his target have been?
evidence: 120 minutes. Day 1: failed at 35. Day 3: quit.
choices: 25 minutes — a small, surmountable step from his measured 20; hit it 4 of 5 sessions, then ratchet to 30. The heroic jump taught him helplessness; the ratchet would have taught him focus.
120 minutes — he just needs more willpower.
10 minutes — aim lower to guarantee success.
No target — targets create pressure; he should just study.
scenarios.why: That he 'can't focus' — a false lesson from a miscalibrated target. Focus trains like a muscle: progressive overload from the measured max. Choice 2 prescribes the willpower that just failed. Choice 3 under-targets (no training stimulus). Choice 4 abandons measurement entirely.
scenarios.hint: What did the 120-minute target teach him?

scenarios.title: The screen break
scenarios.situation: Between 50-minute study blocks, Jordan 'rests' by scrolling feeds for 15 minutes. He returns to the next block feeling foggy and irritable, and his afternoon sessions keep shrinking.
scenarios.prompt: Why aren't his breaks restoring him?
choices: Scrolling is stimulation, not recovery — feeds demand attention and emotional processing, spending the resource breaks should restore; real breaks are movement, water, daylight, distance from screens.
15 minutes is too short — he needs 30-minute scrolls.
He needs a better feed — more relaxing content.
Breaks are the problem — he should power through without them.
scenarios.why: Continuing cognitive work under the label of rest — attention, novelty, and emotion all draw on the same depleted resources. He returns foggy because he never rested. Choice 2 lengthens the depletion. Choice 3 curates the depletion. Choice 4 removes the recovery the system needs.
scenarios.hint: What is a feed-scroll break actually doing?

scenarios.title: The fake rest day
scenarios.situation: Every Sunday is Elena's 'rest day' — during which she does 'just a light review' of flashcards and 'a quick' scenario block. Monday she feels no fresher than Friday. Her dread of the desk is growing.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with her rest day?
evidence: No fresher. Growing dread of the desk.
choices: It is a study day lying about itself — 'light' review still spends attention and prevents genuine recovery; a real rest day has zero study, and her growing dread is recovery debt signaling the system needs actual rest, not disguised work.
Nothing — light review on rest days is efficient.
She needs two rest days — one is insufficient.
Dread is normal — she should push through it.
scenarios.why: Recovery debt — the system is under-rested, and the fake rest days never pay it down. Dread of the desk is a leading indicator; grinding through it deepens the debt. Choice 2 defends the fake rest. Choice 3 adds quantity to a quality problem. Choice 4 prescribes more of what caused it.
scenarios.hint: What is the dread telling her?

scenarios.title: The frameless evening
scenarios.situation: Each evening, Theo sits down to 'study.' No plan, no timer, no shutdown. Three hours pass; he can't say what he accomplished. Some evenings are great, most evaporate. He calls it 'going with the flow.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the frame buying that he lacks?
evidence: 3 hours, no plan, no timer, no shutdown.
choices: Legibility — a 2-minute plan (what/why/target), a defined interval, and a shutdown (done/next) make the session evaluable; without the frame, good evenings are accidents and bad ones teach nothing. 'Flow' without structure is just drift.
Nothing — structure kills creativity; flow is better.
He needs longer evenings — 3 hours is too short.
He should study in the morning — evenings are the problem.
scenarios.why: Because they were undesigned — with no plan and no shutdown, there is no record of what made them work, so they cannot be repeated deliberately. The frame converts luck into method. Choice 2 romanticizes drift. Choice 3 adds hours to illegibility. Choice 4 relocates the same framelessness.
scenarios.hint: Why can't he replicate his great evenings?

scenarios.title: The skipped workout
scenarios.situation: To 'save time' for exam prep, Ana drops her daily 30-minute run. Two weeks later: afternoon focus is worse, sleep is worse, and her total effective study has dropped despite more hours at the desk.
scenarios.prompt: What did the trade actually cost?
evidence: -30 min run, +30 min desk time daily.
Focus worse, sleep worse, effective study down. Hours up.
choices: Net learning — exercise improves attention and encoding for hours and supports sleep; the 'saved' 30 minutes bought depleted desk time while forfeiting the physiological foundation of focus. The run was study preparation, not time away from studying.
Nothing — exercise is unrelated to studying; something else caused the decline.
She should run longer — 30 minutes was insufficient.
She needs to study even more hours to compensate.
scenarios.why: Funding it — aerobic exercise measurably improves subsequent attention, encoding, and sleep quality. Removing it while adding desk hours is borrowing from the foundation to decorate the roof. Choice 2 denies the physiology. Choice 3 misses the point (she removed it entirely). Choice 4 deepens the deficit.
scenarios.hint: What was the run doing for her studying?

domains.name: Test-Taking Tactics: Exam Strategy
domains.description: Parsing questions under pressure, elimination, time budgeting and triage, anxiety control, and the final review pass.

scenarios.title: The missed NOT
scenarios.situation: On a timed mock, Sara answers: 'Which of the following is NOT a desirable difficulty?' She picks 'spaced retrieval practice' — a desirable difficulty — because it looked familiar and correct. She loses the point.
scenarios.prompt: What was her error, and what ritual prevents it?
evidence: 'Which of the following is NOT a desirable difficulty?'
choices: She answered the un-negated question — the prompt asked for the NON-example, and familiarity pulled her to a true statement; the parsing ritual (second pass circling NOT/EXCEPT, restating the task before viewing choices) makes the inversion visible.
She didn't know the material — more studying would fix it.
The question was unfair — NOT questions should be banned.
She was too slow — speed would have saved her.
scenarios.why: Pulled her toward a true-but-wrong answer — the distractor pattern 'true but irrelevant (to the asked question)' working exactly as designed. She knew the content; she misread the task. Choice 2 misdiagnoses knowledge for parsing. Choice 3 rejects a standard format. Choice 4 prescribes the haste that causes such misses.
scenarios.hint: What did familiarity do to her here?

scenarios.title: The wrestled question
scenarios.situation: On question 8 of 60, Mike gets stuck. He spends 9 minutes wrestling it, finally guessing. He then rushes the last 12 questions in 8 minutes, missing several he 'definitely knew.' Final score: just below passing.
scenarios.prompt: What lost him the exam?
evidence: Q8: 9 minutes, guessed. Last 12 questions: 8 minutes, rushed.
choices: Sunk-cost wrestling — 9 minutes on one stuck question stole time from 12 answerable ones; the mark-and-move rule (2x budget max on first pass, return later) would have banked those points and given Q8 a fresh-eyes second look.
Q8 — it was just too hard; nothing could be done.
The last 12 questions — they were unfairly hard.
He needs to think faster — speed is the issue.
scenarios.why: Twelve rushed questions — the exam rewards total points, and one heroic stand cost him a dozen bankable ones. Mark-and-move isn't giving up; it's triage, and the fresh-eyes return often solves the stuck question anyway. Choice 2 excuses the strategy. Choice 3 blames the questions. Choice 4 prescribes haste, which caused the damage.
scenarios.hint: What was the real price of those 9 minutes?

scenarios.title: The blank with no penalty
scenarios.situation: The exam has no guessing penalty. Lena leaves 7 questions blank — 'I didn't want to put a wrong answer.' She scores 68%; passing is 70%. Two of the blanks she could have narrowed to 50/50.
scenarios.prompt: What did the blanks cost her?
evidence: She had narrowed them to two choices each.
choices: The exam — two 50/50 guesses had strong odds of producing the 2 points she needed; with no penalty, expected value of guessing is always positive, and elimination turns guesses into educated ones.
Nothing — wrong answers would have hurt her score.
Her confidence — she should feel good about honest blanks.
Time — she wasted time deciding to skip.
scenarios.why: Positive — half a point per question on average, versus zero for a blank. Two such guesses likely pass her. 'Not wanting a wrong answer' is a feeling; the math is indifferent to feelings. Choice 2 misunderstands no-penalty scoring. Choice 3 moralizes a math error. Choice 4 is trivially true but misses the point.
scenarios.hint: What is the expected value of a 50/50 guess with no penalty?

scenarios.title: The anxiety spiral
scenarios.situation: Five minutes into the exam, Omar's heart is racing and the first question looks alien. He re-reads it four times, understanding less each time. Panic builds. He considers leaving.
scenarios.prompt: What should he do right now?
evidence: Racing heart, alien question, 4 re-reads, rising panic.
4-7-8 breathing, skip to confident questions, bank wins; the spike passes in ~10 min.
choices: Regulate the body first — two cycles of 4-7-8 breathing, then skip the alien question and answer three confident ones; the first-10-minutes spike is physiological and passes once he is working, but re-reading in panic feeds it.
Keep re-reading — understanding will come.
Leave — he is clearly not ready.
Ask the proctor for help with the question.
scenarios.why: Feeding it — each failed re-read confirms the catastrophe narrative, escalating the sympathetic response. The body must be addressed before the mind: breathing down-regulates the physiology, and easy wins prove competence to the panicking brain. Choice 2 repeats the failing action. Choice 3 surrenders to weather. Choice 4 misunderstands the proctor's role.
scenarios.hint: What is the re-reading doing to his panic?

scenarios.title: The gut-change
scenarios.situation: With 3 minutes left, Priya reviews her answers and gets a bad feeling about Q12. No new reading, no spotted error — just unease. She changes it. Later: her original answer was right.
scenarios.prompt: What rule would have saved the point?
evidence: Q12 flipped on unease alone. No re-read evidence.
Original was correct. The change cost a point.
choices: Evidence-gated changes — flip an answer only when re-reading reveals something concrete (a missed NOT, a recognized distractor pattern); 'feels wrong' is anxiety, not data, and anxiety-driven changes hurt more than they help.
Never change answers — first instincts are always right.
Always change answers you feel uneasy about — the gut knows.
She should not review at all — reviews cause damage.
scenarios.why: Anxiety — not insight. The research pattern: changes from re-reading and reasoning tend to help; changes from gut feelings tend to hurt. Priya's flip had no evidentiary basis, so it was a coin flip weighted by nerves. Choice 2 overcorrects into never-changing (re-read evidence does justify changes). Choice 3 sanctifies the gut. Choice 4 abandons the valuable review.
scenarios.hint: What was the unease actually signaling?

scenarios.title: The story answer
scenarios.situation: A scenario describes a struggling student in vivid detail — late nights, crying, a sick parent. The question asks for the best study intervention. David picks 'take a full week off to recover' — moved by the story — though the evidence points to a spacing problem.
scenarios.prompt: What did he answer instead of the question?
evidence: Vivid hardship narrative; evidence shows massed cramming, no spacing.
'Take a week off' — compassionate, unresponsive to the evidence.
choices: The story's emotion — the narrative is context, and the tested decision is the study intervention; stripping the story to the decision ('what fixes massed cramming?') points to spaced retrieval, not the compassionate-but-irrelevant choice.
Correctly — compassion is the best intervention.
He should have picked the longest answer — longest is usually right.
Story questions are unfair — they manipulate emotions.
scenarios.why: Providing context around a decision — and testing whether you can find the decision inside the story. David responded to the character's pain instead of the protocol question. The exam rewards the disciplined reader: what is the actual choice being tested? Choice 2 confuses therapy with test-taking. Choice 3 invokes a myth. Choice 4 rejects the format instead of mastering it.
scenarios.hint: What is the narrative doing in a scenario question?
objectives: Answer the decision, not the story
Strip narrative to the tested choice

scenarios.title: The half-right trap
scenarios.situation: Choice C reads: 'Spaced repetition works because expanding intervals match the forgetting curve — so cram everything the night before.' Ravi picks it: 'the first half is exactly right!'
scenarios.prompt: Why is C wrong?
evidence: 'Spaced repetition works because expanding intervals match the forgetting curve — so cram everything the night before.'
choices: It is half-right — the mechanism is correct but the conclusion ('cram the night before') contradicts it; distractors are built this way deliberately, which is why you must read every choice to its final word before selecting.
It is fully right — Ravi should trust his instinct.
The first half being right means the choice is right — partial credit logic.
These questions are rigged — half-right choices shouldn't exist.
scenarios.why: They borrow credibility — the correct first half disarms scrutiny, and the reader who stops early never meets the fatal second half. Ravi's 'exactly right!' was about half a sentence. The discipline: read to the period, every choice, every time. Choice 2 surrenders to the trap. Choice 3 invents partial-credit logic the exam doesn't use. Choice 4 complains about the game instead of learning its moves.
scenarios.hint: What makes half-right choices so effective as distractors?

scenarios.title: No budget, no checkpoints
scenarios.situation: Nadia 'works steadily' through her 90-minute, 45-question exam with no time plan. At minute 80 she discovers 15 questions remaining. She rushes, mis-bubbles two, and leaves one blank.
scenarios.prompt: What was missing?
choices: Arithmetic — 90 minutes / 45 questions = 2 min each with a 10-minute reserve, plus checkpoints (1/3 time → 1/3 done); without numbers, slow questions hid until minute 80, when recovery was impossible.
Speed — she is just a slow test-taker.
Luck — the questions were front-loaded with hard ones.
Steadiness — she should have worked more steadily.
scenarios.why: Long before minute 80 — it was lost when she started without a budget, because no checkpoint ever warned her. 'Working steadily' without numbers is drifting with confidence. Choice 2 treats a planning failure as a trait. Choice 3 blames distribution. Choice 4 prescribes more of the undefined thing that failed.
scenarios.hint: When did her exam actually get lost?
objectives: Compute and follow a time budget

domains.description: The 48-hour countdown, sleep/food/caffeine protocol, testing-center logistics, and the post-exam review that compounds every attempt.

scenarios.title: The 2am finale
scenarios.situation: The night before his exam, Kevin studies until 2am — 'one more pass through everything.' He sleeps 4 hours, drinks three coffees, and arrives wired. By question 20 he is foggy and misreading prompts.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong, and what was the protocol?
choices: He traded consolidation for familiarity — the 2am cram added unconsolidated exposure while the 4-hour sleep destroyed encoding and the triple caffeine mimicked anxiety; the protocol ends new learning 48h out, protects 8h sleep, and keeps caffeine normal.
He didn't study enough — 2am shows dedication; the fog is unrelated.
He needed four coffees — three was insufficient.
Some people just test badly — nothing to do with the eve.
scenarios.why: Unconsolidated familiarity at the price of the two things the exam needed: a consolidated brain and a rested one. The 48-hour countdown exists because the eve is for arriving, not learning. Choice 2 mistakes dedication for effectiveness. Choice 3 prescribes more of the poison. Choice 4 fatalizes a preventable failure.
scenarios.hint: What did the 'one more pass' actually buy him?

scenarios.title: The unknown building
scenarios.situation: Maria never checked the testing center location. Exam morning: wrong parking lot, 20 minutes lost, rushed check-in, a dispute about her ID. She starts the exam with her heart pounding and never settles.
scenarios.prompt: What fed her anxiety all exam long?
evidence: Wrong lot, 20 min lost, ID dispute, rushed start.
choices: Avoidable logistics unknowns — every one was resolvable the day before (route, parking, ID requirements); the T-24h logistics check exists because anxiety feeds on uncertainty, and her morning manufactured it.
Test anxiety disorder — she needs clinical help.
The exam's difficulty — logistics don't affect performance.
Bad luck — traffic is unpredictable.
scenarios.why: All of the chaos — the route, the parking, and the ID check were knowable 24 hours earlier. She paid for preventable uncertainty with a 3-hour anxiety tax. Choice 2 medicalizes a planning failure. Choice 3 denies that physiology affects cognition. Choice 4 excuses what a checklist prevents.
scenarios.hint: Which part of her morning was actually optional?

scenarios.title: The forum spiral
scenarios.situation: In the testing center lobby, Jamal reads forum posts: 'hardest exam ever,' 'failed twice,' 'trick questions everywhere.' He walks in convinced he will fail. His first 10 minutes are a panic.
scenarios.prompt: What did the forums give him?
evidence: 30 min of failure stories and horror threads.
choices: Other people's panic — unrepresentative (failures post more than passes), unactionable, and perfectly timed to spike his arousal; the protocol says no forums in the final 48h: execute your plan, not the crowd's fear.
Valuable intelligence — he should have read more.
Realistic expectations — the exam IS that hard.
Motivation — fear is a good motivator.
scenarios.why: Failures post disproportionately — the lobby reader samples the worst outcomes and mistakes them for the base rate. Even accurate horror stories are unactionable at T-30 minutes; they can only raise arousal past the productive zone. Choice 2 wants more poison. Choice 3 accepts the biased sample as truth. Choice 4 mistakes panic for fuel.
scenarios.hint: What is the selection bias in exam forums?

scenarios.title: The failed debrief
scenarios.situation: Omar fails his exam at 68%. He tells himself 'the questions were unfair,' books no debrief, and either (a) immediately re-books for next week in despair, or (b) avoids thinking about it for two months. Both happened to friends of his.
scenarios.prompt: What should he do in the next 24 hours?
evidence: Re-book next week, no changes. Path B: avoid for 2 months.
choices: Write the debrief: cluster the misses (topic? format? time? anxiety?), compare prep to what the exam actually tested, design the repair sequence, and let the debrief set the re-take date — not despair (too soon, unchanged) or avoidance (never).
Re-book immediately — momentum matters.
Wait two months — he needs to recover emotionally.
Complain to the test provider — unfair questions must be challenged.
scenarios.why: No diagnosis — A repeats the failure faster, B delays it indefinitely, but neither knows what failed. The 24-hour debrief converts tuition-paid failure into a repair plan; emotion gets 48 hours, then the protocol decides. Choice 2 is path A. Choice 3 is path B. Choice 4 outsources the analysis that only his data can provide.
scenarios.hint: What do paths A and B have in common?
objectives: Let data set the re-take plan

scenarios.title: The passed-and-done
scenarios.situation: Priya passes her exam. 'Done!' She never writes a debrief — 'why analyze a win?' Six months later, preparing for the next certification, she cannot remember what worked: her study system has to be reinvented from scratch.
scenarios.prompt: What did skipping the debrief cost her?
evidence: Next cert prep: system reinvented from zero.
choices: Transferable knowledge — the debrief captures which techniques, schedules, and tactics actually worked, making the protocol evidence-based and reusable; without it, every certification starts from scratch and past tuition is wasted.
Nothing — a pass is a pass; analysis is for failures.
Time — the debrief would have wasted an hour.
Humility — winners don't need review.
scenarios.why: An unrecorded experiment — the outcome is known but the causes are not, so nothing transfers to the next challenge. The capstone protocol document is built from exactly these debriefs. Choice 2 treats wins as unanalyzable luck. Choice 3 prices an hour against reinventing a system. Choice 4 confuses review with self-criticism.
scenarios.hint: What is a pass without a debrief?

scenarios.title: The broken station
scenarios.situation: Mid-exam, Lena's workstation freezes twice; the timer keeps running. She tries to power through, losing 10 minutes, growing frantic. She says nothing until after the exam.
scenarios.prompt: What should she have done at the first freeze?
choices: Stopped, raised her hand, and documented — testing centers have procedures for technical failures (pauses, restarts, incident reports), but only if invoked during the exam; silent suffering forfeits the remedy.
Powered through — reporting disrupts focus more than the freeze.
Restarted the computer herself — faster than waiting.
Accepted it — tech issues are part of the test.
scenarios.why: The remedy — incident procedures exist but require contemporaneous reporting; post-exam complaints about unreported issues rarely succeed. Ten minutes and a frantic state, both recoverable if she had raised her hand at freeze one. Choice 2 values uninterrupted focus over 10 lost minutes. Choice 3 risks voiding the session. Choice 4 normalizes forfeiting her rights.
scenarios.hint: What did her silence cost her?

lessons.title: The Deep Work Study Protocol — Core concepts
concepts: A curriculum is a delivery system for attention. Most online learning is engineered against the learner — feeds, autoplay, streaks fragment the attention the material requires; this protocol inverts every one of those choices.

Distraction-free by design: long-form module pages, no feed, no recommendations, no autoplay, no notification layer. The missing features are missing deliberately — a learning platform should earn its place by serving deep work, and every feature that doesn't is a liability.

The contract has two parties: the site never manufactures a distraction; the learner brings the device rules — notifications off, phone in another room, one tab open. The page cannot silence your phone.
The study rhythm: one module, one deep session. The module's length is deliberate — cognitively demanding material needs unbroken time — and the session ends when the module ends.
Attention training is part of the curriculum: focus is treated as a trainable skill with targets that ratchet up, not as a fixed trait or a matter of willpower.
Depth metrics: done means artifacts, not hours. Labs completed, proofs re-derived, systems built — hours measure exposure, artifacts measure capability, and only capability compounds.
Slow-productivity pacing: fewer obligations, natural pace, obsessive quality. Sustainable depth across a semester beats sprint-and-burn; cramming produces familiarity that evaporates.

example.code:
mkdir -p ~/protocol && cat > ~/protocol/my-protocol.md <<'EOF'
# My 90-day study protocol
## 1. Environment contract
- Phone in another room, notifications off, one tab open.
## 2. Rhythm
- One module, one deep session. Session ends when the module ends.
## 3. Attention training
- Deep-hour target: 8/week, +1 every 2 weeks. Boredom practice: no phone in queues.
## 4. Depth metric (artifacts, NOT hours)
- Weekly artifact quota: 2. This week's: ___, ___
## 5. Pacing
- Fixed shutdown 21:30. Max 2 active tracks. Quarterly artifact review.
EOF
cat ~/protocol/my-protocol.md
example.walkthrough: Write the five commitments as mechanisms, not aspirations: environment rules, session boundaries, ratcheting attention targets, a weekly artifact quota with hours explicitly excluded, and pacing guardrails. The file is the protocol — review it weekly against the artifacts you actually produced.

pitfalls: Common trap: keeping the site's half of the contract while breaking yours. A distraction-free page plus a buzzing phone is still a distracted session.
Common trap: 'modules touched' as progress. Half-modules and interleaved tracks break the rhythm and the dependency chain.
Common trap: optimizing hours. Any system that rewards input gets input optimized and output faked — count artifacts.
Common trap: sprint-and-burn pacing dressed up as ambition. Depth compounds under consistent load; cramming evaporates.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab: run a distraction-free session audit, then write your 90-day protocol with artifact quotas.

lessons.title: Lesson Sequences — Core concepts
concepts: A lesson sequence is the lesson layer under every learning path: an ordered progression of modules where each step's prerequisites are satisfied by earlier steps. Order is pedagogy, not packaging.

Dependency order is the only honest ordering. Alphabetical, by-publication, or difficulty-shuffled orders strand the learner; every module implicitly asserts what the learner can now do, and the chain must make that assertion true.
One module, one deep session: each module gets unbroken time, a lab producing an artifact, and a self-check gate before the next module builds on it. The gates are what make the chain trustworthy.
Capstones synthesize at the end. Early modules motivate through small completable wins; placing synthesis early produces frustration, not momentum. A sequence that never synthesizes is a playlist.
Prerequisites are structural, not advisory. 'Optional background' is where dependency chains die — promote the prerequisite, add a verifiable gate, then unlock the downstream module.

Design backward from the capstone artifact: the end state defines the chain, the chain defines the modules. Remix across sequences only by re-deriving the full dependency chain and re-validating every gate.

example.code:
mkdir -p ~/sequences && cat > ~/sequences/tf-sequence.md <<'EOF'
# Terraform & IaC — 8-module sequence (backward-designed)
# Capstone: versioned, reviewed, applied multi-env setup
1. HCL syntax & resource blocks        [lab: first config, artifact: main.tf]
2. State: what it is, why it bites       [lab: state surgery in sandbox]
3. plan/apply workflow                  [lab: plan review drill, gate: read a plan]
4. Variables, outputs, modules          [lab: refactor to module, artifact]
5. Remote backends & locking            [lab: team backend setup]
6. Workspaces vs directory-per-env      [lab: two-env layout, gate: justify choice]
7. Testing & policy (validate/test/sentinel) [lab: policy gate]
8. CAPSTONE: multi-env reviewed apply   [artifact: repo + runbook]
# Rule: module N's prerequisites all live in modules < N.
EOF
cat ~/sequences/tf-sequence.md
example.walkthrough: Sketch the sequence as a dependency-ordered list, each line carrying its lab artifact and any gate. The trailing rule is the whole discipline in one line: nothing in module N may assume knowledge that only appears later. Write it, then audit it by deleting each module and asking what breaks.

pitfalls: Common trap: ordering by topic popularity instead of dependency. Interesting-first strands learners at the first hard prerequisite.
Common trap: 'optional background' prerequisites. If a downstream module needs it, it is required — make it a module with a gate.
Common trap: capstone-as-teaser. Synthesis belongs at the end; early motivation comes from completable wins.
Common trap: counting clicked modules as completed. Done means artifacts produced and gates passed, not pages visited.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab: map the dependency chain of a sequence you care about, then backward-design your own 6-module sequence.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Study Protocol move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence
lessons.try_it: Pick any process in this course. Write out the full journey from trigger to outcome, naming every system touched.

lessons.title: Welcome: What This Bootcamp Is and Isn't
concepts: This bootcamp teaches a study method, not a subject. The domains are the curriculum of learning itself: memory, recall, spacing, notes, focus, and exam execution. You master the protocol by applying it to whatever you are actually studying.

The method is evidence-based. Retrieval practice, spaced repetition, interleaving, and elaboration each rest on decades of cognitive-science research — this is not productivity folklore or motivational content.

You are assessed the way the real world assesses you: scenario questions that ask you to apply the protocol to realistic situations, plus hands-on labs that produce artifacts. Passive reading alone cannot pass.
There is no shortcut here. No technique replaces effort. What the protocol does is convert your effort into durable learning instead of letting it evaporate the way re-reading and highlighting do.

Run this bootcamp in parallel with a real target — a certification, an exam, a course. The labs will ask you to use your actual study material, and the protocol only works on material you genuinely need to learn.

example.code:
Worked example — Ana applies the protocol to a cloud certification
Setup: Ana has 60 days until her exam and a 400-page study guide.
Naive approach: read the guide twice, highlight, hope.
Protocol approach: she converts each chapter into atomic flashcards (active recall), schedules them on expanding intervals (spacing), mixes chapters in review sessions (interleaving), and explains each service aloud as if teaching it (Feynman).
Result: same 60 days, but every hour of effort lands in long-term memory instead of short-term familiarity.
example.walkthrough: Read the setup and name which protocol layer each action belongs to before checking the takeaway. Then compare your answer: did you catch all four techniques?

pitfalls: Common trap: treating the bootcamp as the thing to study — the bootcamp is the method; your exam material is the content the method runs on.
Common trap: assuming evidence-based means effortless — the techniques work precisely because they are effortful; ease is the enemy.
Common trap: collecting techniques like trophies — one protocol, run consistently, beats ten techniques sampled once.
Common trap: skipping the labs because you 'get the idea' — the labs are where the method becomes a habit; ideas without reps do not transfer.
lessons.try_it: Before the next lesson, write down the one exam or skill you will apply this protocol to, plus your target date. Everything you build from here attaches to that target.

lessons.title: How to Navigate the Bootcamp
concepts: Three content types, one loop. Lessons teach the concept with worked examples. Scenarios test application under realistic conditions. Labs turn the concept into a physical artifact. The loop is: learn it, apply it, build it.

Domains are ordered deliberately: Start Here first, then the science (memory), then the core techniques (recall, spacing, notes), then the deep-processing layer (elaboration, metacognition), then performance (focus, test tactics, exam day). Follow the order on your first pass.
Each domain ends with 5-8 scenarios. Treat them as diagnostics, not homework: a wrong answer is data about which concept to re-study, not a failure.

The Mock Assessment domain draws scenarios from every domain at runtime — it is your dress rehearsal. Take it under real timed conditions when you finish the domains, and again after your weak-spot pass.

Your progress is measured in artifacts: labs completed, decks built, error logs maintained, a capstone protocol document. If you cannot point at artifacts, you have not done the bootcamp — you have browsed it.

example.code:
Worked example — the weekly loop in practice
Monday: new lessons (2-3), one deep session each.
Tuesday–Thursday: scenario blocks from the same domains, error log updated after each block.
Friday: labs — build the artifacts (decks, notes, sequences).
Weekend: spaced review of everything + one synthesis artifact.
Why it works: every content type appears every week, so nothing decays, and the error log steers next week's focus.
example.walkthrough: Map one real week of your calendar onto this loop before checking the walkthrough. Which day is your lab day?

pitfalls: Common trap: doing all lessons first, then all scenarios — interleaving content types beats batching them.
Common trap: re-taking scenarios you already passed instead of attacking the ones you failed — comfort reps feel productive and are not.
Common trap: treating the mock assessment as a final exam — it is a diagnostic instrument; take it early enough to act on it.
Common trap: confusing motion with progress — hours logged mean nothing; count artifacts and scenario accuracy instead.
lessons.try_it: Open your calendar and block the loop for next week: lesson days, scenario days, lab day, review day. Make the blocks real appointments.

lessons.title: Your Study Plan: The 90-Day Map
concepts: Phase 1 — Foundation (weeks 1–3): complete Start Here, Memory Science, Active Recall, and Spaced Repetition. Build your first flashcard deck and your Leitner box. Output: a working review system.

Phase 2 — Practice (weeks 4–8): finish Note Systems, Elaboration, Metacognition, and Focus Management. Run scenarios weekly; keep an error log; synthesize notes into artifacts. Output: rising scenario accuracy and a full error log.

Phase 3 — Peak (weeks 9–12): Test-Taking Tactics and Exam-Day Performance, then the mock assessment under timed conditions, then a targeted weak-spot pass. Output: mock scores at or above your target, then the capstone.
Weekly rhythm inside every phase: lessons introduce, scenarios diagnose, labs build, spaced review protects. The rhythm never changes; only the content does.
Plans are hypotheses. After week 3, re-plan from your data: scenario accuracy by domain, error-log patterns, and review load. A plan that ignores your data is decoration.

example.code:
Worked example — re-planning from data
After week 3, Devon's accuracy: memory science 90%, active recall 85%, spaced repetition 55%.
Re-plan: he keeps the phase-2 lesson schedule but adds a daily 15-minute spacing-repair block and rebuilds his Leitner box with shorter intervals.
Takeaway: the data said spacing was the leak; the plan changed to fix the leak, not to 'study harder' in general.
example.walkthrough: Look at your own weakest domain so far and write the one plan change it implies. Specific beats vague: '15-minute repair block' beats 'review more.'

pitfalls: Common trap: front-loading all the lessons — the protocol is a practice system; lessons without weekly reps decay.
Common trap: planning in hours instead of artifacts — 'study 10 hours' is not a plan; 'build 60 cards and clear the box' is.
Common trap: never re-planning — a 90-day plan written on day 1 is guaranteed wrong by day 21; schedule the re-plan.
Common trap: skipping Phase 3's weak-spot pass — the mock tells you where to aim; skipping the pass wastes the diagnostic.
lessons.try_it: Draft your own 90-day map in one page: three phases, weekly rhythm, and the date of your first mock assessment.

lessons.title: How You'll Be Assessed
concepts: Scenario questions mirror real exam pressure: a situation, evidence to interpret, a prompt, four choices, one best answer. They test judgment under uncertainty, not memorized definitions.
Every scenario has a hint and a full explanation. Use the hint when stuck — it costs nothing — but read the explanation after every answer, right or wrong. The explanation is the lesson.

Labs are assessed on artifacts, not effort claims. Each lab lists checks: concrete verifiable conditions (a file exists, a deck has N cards, an error log has dated entries). You pass when the artifacts exist.
The mock assessment is timed and cumulative. Its job is to find your weakest domains before the real exam does. A low mock score is a gift — it is a map.

Passing standard for this bootcamp: complete all labs, score consistently on scenarios across domains, and produce the capstone protocol document. Certificates come from your real exam; this bootcamp gives you the machine that earns them.

example.code:
Worked example — reading an explanation after a wrong answer
Devon picks 're-read the chapter' on a spacing scenario and gets it wrong.
The explanation: re-reading feels fluent because of familiarity, but fluency is not retrievability; the correct move is a retrieval attempt after a delay.
Devon adds 'fluency trap' to his error log and re-tests the concept with blank-page recall the next day.
example.walkthrough: After your next wrong scenario answer, write the explanation's core claim in your own words before moving on. That single sentence is the real lesson.

pitfalls: Common trap: skipping explanations on correct answers — a right answer for the wrong reason is a future wrong answer.
Common trap: treating hints as cheating — hints model the reasoning moves the exam rewards; use them deliberately.
Common trap: lab-check gaming — faking an artifact to pass a check only defrauds the one person the protocol serves.
Common trap: one mock and done — take the mock, repair, re-take. The second score is the one that predicts the exam.
lessons.try_it: Set your personal passing bar in writing: target mock score, labs complete by date, capstone deadline. Sign it.

lessons.title: Protocol Layer 2: The Attention Ledger
concepts: The attention ledger is a running account of where your focus actually went. Each session you log: deep minutes, interruptions, and what caused them. You cannot manage what you do not measure.
Log immediately after the session, not from memory at day's end. Memory edits the record — 'it was only one quick check' becomes the story even when the phone ate twenty minutes.
Review the ledger weekly. Patterns beat anecdotes: the same interruption source three weeks running is a system problem, not a willpower problem, and system problems get system fixes.
The ledger's second column is artifacts produced. Attention without artifacts is entertainment; the ledger proves whether the two-party contract converted focus into capability.
Keep the ledger boring and permanent: one file, one format, dated entries. A beautiful tracking system you abandon in week two is worse than a plain text file you keep.

example.code:
Worked example — ledger entry
Date: 2026-10-12 | Module: spaced-repetition L3 | Deep minutes: 55 | Interruptions: 2 (phone buzz x1, tab-switch x1) | Artifacts: 12 flashcards built.
Weekly review: phone buzzes cluster on mornings after late nights → system fix: phone charges in the kitchen, alarm clock purchased.
Takeaway: the ledger turned a vague 'I get distracted' into a specific fixable cause.
example.walkthrough: Write one ledger entry for your last real study session from memory, then note which fields you had to guess. Those guesses are what the ledger fixes.

pitfalls: Common trap: logging only good sessions — the ledger's value is in the bad ones; missing entries are data too.
Common trap: over-engineering the format — if logging takes more than two minutes, you will quit; keep it minimal.
Common trap: reviewing without acting — a pattern you notice and ignore is just guilt with extra steps.
Common trap: confusing deep minutes with clock minutes — a 90-minute session with 30 interruptions is not 90 deep minutes.
lessons.try_it: Create your attention ledger file today with the five columns, and log your next three sessions in it.

lessons.title: Protocol Layer 3: Spacing and Interleaving Inside the Protocol
concepts: The protocol's study rhythm is one module per deep session — but the review rhythm is spaced and interleaved. New material gets focus; old material gets retrieval on expanding intervals.

Interleaving means mixing domains inside a review session: a memory-science scenario, then a test-tactics scenario, then a note-systems scenario. Mixing feels harder than blocking — that difficulty is the mechanism.

The weekly synthesis session is interleaving at the artifact level: you connect this week's concepts to prior weeks' notes, forcing retrieval across the whole curriculum instead of the current chapter.
Sequence design follows the same rule: never schedule two same-domain deep sessions back-to-back in review weeks. The brain discriminates better when it must choose which tool to use.

Spacing protects against the fluency trap: material reviewed too soon feels easy and teaches nothing. The protocol's intervals are deliberately uncomfortable — discomfort is the signal that retrieval is real.

example.code:
Worked example — an interleaved review session
Session plan: 10 scenarios each from memory-science, active-recall, and test-taking-tactics, shuffled.
Blocked alternative: 30 memory-science scenarios in a row.
Outcome: blocked feels smoother; interleaved produces 20% higher accuracy on the next mock because the brain practiced choosing, not just executing.
example.walkthrough: Build one interleaved review session from three domains you have studied. Shuffle them. Note how it feels compared to blocked practice.

pitfalls: Common trap: interleaving brand-new material — interleave only after initial learning; mixing what you have never learned is confusion, not desirable difficulty.
Common trap: spacing so wide you re-learn instead of retrieve — if accuracy collapses below ~70%, tighten the interval.
Common trap: mistaking the discomfort of interleaving for 'this isn't working' — the feeling of difficulty is the feeling of learning.
Common trap: blocking because the platform defaults to it — the protocol's order is a default, not a law; shuffle your reviews.
lessons.try_it: Schedule this week's review as one interleaved session across three domains and log the accuracy difference versus your last blocked session.

lessons.title: Protocol Layer 4: The Weekly Artifact Review
concepts: The weekly review is a 30-minute ritual with three questions: what artifacts did I produce, what does my error log say, and what changes next week. Same time, same place, every week.
Artifacts first: count decks, notes, lab outputs, protocol documents. The count is the honest measure of the week — hours are self-reported, artifacts are verifiable.
Error log second: group this week's misses by concept, not by question. Three misses on 'spacing intervals' is one problem with one fix; ten scattered misses is a review-load problem.
The output of the review is a written plan change — one or two sentences, specific. 'Add a 15-minute spacing-repair block on Tuesdays' beats 'study harder next week.'
Archive the review notes. Twelve weeks of reviews is a dataset about how you learn — it becomes the raw material for your capstone protocol document.

example.code:
Worked example — a review that changed the plan
Artifacts: 40 cards, 1 synthesis note, 2 labs. Error log: 5 misses, 4 on interleaving.
Plan change: replace Friday's blocked review with an interleaved session; re-test interleaving scenarios in 7 days.
Next week's review: interleaving misses dropped to 1. The ritual worked because it ended in a specific change.
example.walkthrough: Run a 30-minute review of your last week right now: artifacts, error patterns, one plan change. Write it down.

pitfalls: Common trap: reviewing without the error log open — memory of the week is as edited as memory of a session; use the data.
Common trap: changing five things at once — one or two changes per week; more than that and you cannot tell what worked.
Common trap: skipping the review when the week went badly — bad weeks are when the review pays the most.
Common trap: no archive — unrecorded reviews evaporate; the capstone needs the dataset.
lessons.try_it: Put a recurring 30-minute weekly review on your calendar now, and create the archive file for the notes.

lessons.title: Sequences: From Modules to Missions
concepts: A module delivers a concept; a mission applies it. Sequences chain modules into missions: learn spaced repetition, then build a Leitner box; learn error logs, then run a calibration quiz.
Design sequences backward from the artifact. Ask: what will the learner hold at the end? Then choose the minimum modules that produce it. Everything else is optional enrichment.
Each link in a sequence has a handoff: the output of one module becomes the input of the next. The Leitner box built in the spacing mission becomes the review engine for every later mission.
Sequences have gates, not grades: you advance when the artifact passes its checks. A gate you can fake is not a gate — checks must be verifiable, like the lab checks in this bootcamp.
Good sequences are short. Three to five links beat ten: each additional link multiplies the chance the learner stalls. Depth comes from revisiting, not from length.

example.code:
Worked example — a 4-link sequence
Link 1: active-recall lesson → Link 2: build 30 atomic cards (artifact) → Link 3: spaced-repetition lesson → Link 4: load cards into Leitner box and run first review (artifact).
Handoffs: cards flow into the box; the box becomes the review engine.
Gate: 30 cards exist and the box has dated compartments.
example.walkthrough: Sketch a 4-link sequence for a topic you are studying: modules, artifacts, handoffs, and one gate.

pitfalls: Common trap: sequences of pure content — a chain of lessons with no artifacts is a playlist, not a sequence.
Common trap: no handoffs — if link 2 does not use link 1's output, the links are independent and the sequence is fake.
Common trap: gates as quizzes about the lesson — gate on the artifact, not on recall of the teaching.
Common trap: the mega-sequence — ten links deep, abandoned at link three; split it into two missions.
lessons.try_it: Convert your current study topic into one 4-link sequence with artifacts and gates, and run link 1 today.

lessons.title: Sequencing for Weak Spots
concepts: Weak-spot sequencing starts from the error log, not from the curriculum. The log's concept clusters become the sequence's targets: each cluster gets a re-learn link, a drill link, and a re-test link.
Order weak spots by leverage: foundational concepts before advanced ones, high-frequency exam topics before rare ones. Fixing a root cause clears multiple symptoms.

The re-learn link must use a different modality than the original learning. If reading produced the miss, re-learn by teaching or by worked example — repeating the failed modality repeats the failure.
Drill links are short and dense: 10-15 targeted scenarios or one focused lab, not a full domain re-run. Surgical beats comprehensive when the diagnosis is specific.
Close the loop: re-test with fresh scenarios on the same concept after a delay. A weak spot is only fixed when delayed retrieval succeeds — immediate re-testing measures short-term memory.

example.code:
Worked example — repairing 'spacing intervals'
Error log: 4 misses on interval timing. Sequence: re-learn via the forgetting-curve worked example (new modality) → drill: 12 spacing scenarios → wait 5 days → re-test: 10 fresh spacing scenarios.
Result: 8/10 on re-test. The weak spot is closed; the log records the fix.
example.walkthrough: Take your top error-log cluster and design its 3-link repair sequence right now.

pitfalls: Common trap: re-running the whole domain — a targeted miss does not need a comprehensive re-run; it needs a targeted sequence.
Common trap: same-modality re-learning — re-reading the lesson you already read is the definition of insanity with extra steps.
Common trap: immediate re-testing — passing today proves nothing; the delay is the test.
Common trap: never closing the loop — a repair sequence without a re-test is a hope, not a fix.
lessons.try_it: Build the repair sequence for your current top weak spot and schedule the delayed re-test date.

lessons.title: Adaptive Sequencing: Reading Your Own Data
concepts: Adaptive sequencing means the next link is chosen by your data, not by the table of contents. Scenario accuracy, error-log clusters, and review load together vote on what comes next.
Set decision rules in advance: if domain accuracy drops below 70%, insert a repair sequence before new material. Rules beat willpower — you follow the rule even when you would rather move on.

Track review load as a hard constraint. Spaced review is a growing obligation; if daily reviews exceed 30 minutes, pause new cards and consolidate. A system that collapses under its own reviews teaches nothing.
Adapt the modality to the miss type: concept misses get re-teaching, application misses get more scenarios, recall misses get tighter spacing. Different failures need different sequences.
Log every adaptation and its result. Over weeks this becomes your personal learning profile — the evidence base your capstone protocol document is built from.

example.code:
Worked example — the 70% rule fires
Week 5: test-taking-tactics accuracy 62%. Rule triggers: pause new lessons, run repair sequence (re-learn via worked examples → 15 scenarios → re-test in 5 days).
Week 6: accuracy 81%. The rule made the decision before motivation could argue.
example.walkthrough: Write your three decision rules now: the accuracy trigger, the review-load cap, and the modality map.

pitfalls: Common trap: adapting on feelings — 'I feel behind' is not data; accuracy and load are data.
Common trap: no pre-set rules — deciding in the moment means deciding with your biases; set rules when calm.
Common trap: adapting too fast — one bad session is noise; adapt on weekly trends, not daily moods.
Common trap: collecting data you never read — the weekly review exists to convert data into decisions.
lessons.try_it: Write your decision rules into your protocol notes and apply the accuracy trigger to this week's plan.

lessons.title: Encoding: Attention Is the Gatekeeper
concepts: Nothing is remembered that was not first attended to. Encoding — the conversion of experience into a memory trace — requires focused attention; divided attention during learning produces traces too weak to retrieve later.

Depth of processing determines durability. Semantic processing (meaning, connections, implications) creates far stronger traces than shallow processing (appearance, repetition, highlighting). Ask 'what does this mean and connect to' not 'what does this say.'

Elaborative encoding links new material to existing knowledge. The richer the network of associations around a trace, the more retrieval routes lead back to it — which is why examples and analogies beat definitions.

Multitasking during study is task-switching, and every switch exacts a cost: the trace formed in the seconds around a switch is fragmented. The phone check does not cost thirty seconds; it costs the encoding of whatever you were learning.
Encoding is the only stage you fully control. You cannot directly command retrieval or consolidation — but you can command undivided, deep, elaborative attention right now.

example.code:
Worked example — two encodings of one concept
Shallow: re-reading 'spaced repetition = expanding intervals' three times.
Deep: asking 'why expanding and not fixed?' → because each successful retrieval at the edge of forgetting strengthens the trace more → connecting to weight training (progressive overload).
Test next week: the shallow trace is gone; the deep trace retrieves with its associations intact.
example.walkthrough: Take one concept from your material and encode it three ways: definition, example, and connection to something you already know. Test yourself tomorrow.

pitfalls: Common trap: equating exposure with encoding — sitting through a lecture with divided attention encodes almost nothing.
Common trap: shallow processing habits — highlighting and re-reading feel like studying but process surface features, not meaning.
Common trap: blaming memory for an attention failure — 'I have a bad memory' usually means 'I studied distracted.'
Common trap: trying to fix retrieval when encoding failed — no retrieval technique recovers what was never encoded; fix the input first.
lessons.try_it: Study your next module with the device rules on and write one elaborative connection per concept — then blank-page recall it tomorrow.

lessons.title: The Forgetting Curve and Why It Matters
concepts: Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve: without review, retention of new material collapses within days — roughly half is gone in the first day, and the curve flattens near zero. Forgetting is the default; remembering requires intervention.

The curve's steepest drop is early, which is why the first review matters most. A retrieval attempt within 24 hours of learning flattens the curve dramatically — this single habit beats most study systems.

Each successful retrieval resets the curve at a shallower slope: the memory becomes more durable with every spaced recall. Forgetting is not the enemy; the edge of forgetting is where strengthening happens.
The curve applies to recognition-resistant knowledge too. You may still 'recognize' material weeks later while being unable to recall it — and exams test recall, not recognition.
Design implication: schedule the first review within a day, the second within a few days, then expand. This is the entire logic of spaced repetition, derived from the curve's shape.

example.code:
Worked example — the 24-hour review
Monday 8pm: learn 20 networking concepts. Tuesday 8pm: blank-page recall before any review — retrieves 9/20, then re-studies the 11 missed.
No-review alternative: by Friday, recall would be ~4/20.
Takeaway: one 15-minute retrieval session within 24 hours more than doubled durable retention.
example.walkthrough: After your next lesson, set a timer for 24 hours later and do a blank-page recall before you allow yourself to re-read anything.

pitfalls: Common trap: reviewing too late — the first review a week later finds the trace nearly gone; you are re-learning, not retrieving.
Common trap: reviewing by re-reading — re-reading resets familiarity, not the curve; only retrieval flattens it.
Common trap: assuming slow forgetting means strong memory — the flat tail of the curve is recognition residue, not recallable knowledge.
Common trap: one-and-done reviewing — a single review helps, but durability comes from repeated spaced retrievals.
lessons.try_it: For everything you learn this week, schedule the 24-hour retrieval before you close the session.

lessons.title: Sleep, Consolidation, and the Two-Day Rule
concepts: Memory consolidation — the stabilization of traces into long-term storage — happens largely during sleep, especially slow-wave sleep. Study creates the trace; sleep files it.
Sleep deprivation impairs both encoding (tired brains attend poorly) and consolidation (less slow-wave sleep, weaker filing). An all-nighter trades tomorrow's retrieval for tonight's familiarity.
The two-day rule: never go more than two days without sleep-protecting your learning — meaning no multi-day cram binges that sacrifice sleep, and no learning scheduled so late that sleep is cut.
Naps count: a 20-90 minute nap after a heavy learning session measurably improves retention versus staying awake. The nap is part of the study session, not a break from it.
Design implication: end study sessions at a consistent hour, protect 7-9 hours, and schedule the hardest encoding for when you are rested — mornings for most people, not midnight.

example.code:
Worked example — the all-nighter audit
Two learners, same 8 hours of material. A sleeps 8 hours after studying; B studies through the night.
Next-day recall: A 72%, B 48%. B also encodes the next day's material 30% worse.
Takeaway: the all-nighter borrows from two days of learning to fund one night of familiarity.
example.walkthrough: Audit your last two weeks: how many sessions ended within an hour of sleep, and how many stole from it?

pitfalls: Common trap: the heroic all-nighter — it feels dedicated and performs terribly; the research is unambiguous.
Common trap: caffeine as sleep replacement — stimulants mask fatigue; they do not restore encoding or consolidation.
Common trap: irregular sleep — consolidation follows circadian rhythm; a chaotic schedule files memories chaotically.
Common trap: studying hardest material when exhausted — match cognitive demand to rested hours.
lessons.try_it: Set a hard study end-time tonight that protects 8 hours of sleep, and move your hardest topic to your most rested hour tomorrow.

lessons.title: Chunking: Building Long-Term Schemas
concepts: Chunking is the brain's compression algorithm: individual items are bound into meaningful units (chunks), and working memory holds chunks, not items. Experts are experts because they have bigger, better-organized chunks.

A schema is a chunk writ large — an organized framework of knowledge (e.g., 'how TCP works') that new details slot into. Learning with a schema is fast; learning without one is memorizing disconnected facts.
Build chunks deliberately: learn the big picture first (the schema skeleton), then attach details to it. Details learned before the schema have nothing to hang on and fall off.
Retrieval builds chunks: every time you recall a concept and its connections, the binding strengthens. This is why explain-backs create understanding — explaining forces chunk assembly.
Chunking has a failure mode: illusory chunks. A vague sense of the big picture without retrievable details is not a schema — test chunks by recalling the details they supposedly organize.

example.code:
Worked example — chunking TCP
Skeleton first: 'TCP = reliable byte stream over unreliable IP via sequence numbers, ACKs, retransmission, flow control.'
Details attach: sequence numbers → ordering; ACKs → confirmation; retransmission → loss recovery; flow control → receiver protection.
Test: blank-page recall of the skeleton, then each detail and its purpose. The skeleton retrieves the details.
example.walkthrough: Take your hardest current topic and write its skeleton in one sentence, then attach five details to it.

pitfalls: Common trap: details-first learning — memorizing facts before the framework; the facts scatter.
Common trap: mistaking recognition of the skeleton for possession of it — if you cannot recall the details, the chunk is hollow.
Common trap: never testing the chunk — chunks feel complete long before they are; retrieval is the audit.
Common trap: one giant chunk — schemas should be hierarchical; a single undifferentiated blob is not organized knowledge.
lessons.try_it: Build a one-page schema map for your current topic: skeleton, branches, details — then recall it blank-page tomorrow.

lessons.title: Desirable Difficulties: Friction That Helps
concepts: Desirable difficulties are learning conditions that slow initial performance but improve long-term retention: spacing, interleaving, retrieval practice, and varied practice all qualify.

'Desirable' has two conditions: the difficulty must engage the right processes (retrieval, discrimination, transfer), and the learner must be able to overcome it. Impossible difficulty is just difficulty.

The paradox: conditions that feel fluent (re-reading, blocked practice, highlighted review) produce high immediate performance and poor retention; conditions that feel effortful produce the reverse. Trust the delayed test, not the feeling.

Introduce difficulty progressively. A beginner needs more guidance and less friction; as schemas build, increase spacing, interleaving, and retrieval demands. Desirable is relative to current capability.
Design implication: when practice feels too smooth, add friction — close the book, shuffle the order, delay the review. Smooth practice is usually a warning sign.

example.code:
Worked example — calibrating difficulty
Week 1: blocked practice, open-book → 90% (too smooth, little retention).
Week 2: interleaved, closed-book, 2-day delay → 65% (hard, strong retention).
Week 3: same as week 2 → 80% (difficulty now desirable: challenging but surmountable, retention high).
Takeaway: tune friction until effort is high and success is possible.
example.walkthrough: Rate your last three study sessions on friction (1=smooth, 5=brutal) and guess which produced the most retention. Then check against a delayed recall.

pitfalls: Common trap: maximizing difficulty — brutal is not desirable; if you cannot succeed, the difficulty is just an obstacle.
Common trap: difficulty without feedback — effortful practice with no correction encodes errors confidently.
Common trap: applying friction to brand-new material — desirable difficulties assume initial learning has happened.
Common trap: quitting at the discomfort — the first interleaved session always feels bad; the feeling is not the verdict.
lessons.try_it: Add one friction upgrade to this week's practice: close the book, shuffle, or delay — and log the result.

lessons.title: Retrieval Practice: The Testing Effect
concepts: The testing effect: retrieving information from memory strengthens the memory far more than re-studying it. A test is not just a measurement of learning — it is one of the most powerful causes of learning.

Retrieval works through effortful reconstruction. The struggle to recall — even unsuccessful attempts — primes the brain to encode the correct answer deeply when it appears. Failed retrieval followed by feedback beats re-study.

Low-stakes frequent retrieval beats high-stakes rare testing. Daily 10-minute self-quizzes produce more durable learning than one big practice exam, because frequency compounds and stakes stay low enough to attempt hard recalls.
Retrieval must be from memory, not from recognition. Multiple-choice-only practice can devolve into recognition; mix in free recall (blank page, no cues) to force genuine reconstruction.
Feedback closes the loop: retrieve, check, correct. Retrieval without feedback risks encoding errors confidently — always verify against the source after the attempt, never before.

example.code:
Worked example — the failed retrieval
Prompt: 'Explain the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption — no notes.'
Attempt: partial, muddled, missing key exchange.
Feedback: checks source, corrects the gap.
Next week: clean recall. The failed attempt was not wasted — it made the feedback stick.
example.walkthrough: Pick one concept and attempt a no-notes explanation right now. Then check the source and note exactly what the attempt missed.

pitfalls: Common trap: testing only after 'ready' — waiting until you feel prepared wastes the testing effect; retrieve early and often, failure included.
Common trap: retrieval without feedback — confident wrong answers are worse than no answers; always verify.
Common trap: recognition disguised as retrieval — re-reading choices until one 'looks right' is not retrieval practice.
Common trap: high-stakes-only testing — one big exam creates anxiety without the compounding benefit of frequent low-stakes reps.
lessons.try_it: End every study session this week with a 10-minute closed-book self-quiz on that session's material — before any review.

lessons.title: Free Recall and the Blank Page
concepts: Free recall: after a study session, close everything and write down everything you remember — no cues, no prompts, no peeking. The blank page is the most honest diagnostic in the protocol.
Score the recall against the source: what did you get, what did you miss, what did you distort? Misses become tomorrow's retrieval targets; distortions become error-log entries.
Free recall forces organization, not just retrieval. To write it down, you must sequence and connect — which is why it builds chunks while testing them.
Start with short windows: recall the last 25-minute session, not the last month. Expand the window as the habit strengthens — session, then day, then week.
The blank page also defeats the fluency trap. Familiarity cannot write paragraphs; only genuine recall can. If the page stays blank, the learning did not happen — and now you know.

example.code:
Worked example — a blank-page session
Study: 25 minutes on spaced intervals. Close book. Write: everything remembered about intervals — 7 points captured, 3 missed (the expansion ratios).
Next: re-study only the 3 missed points, then a second blank-page attempt tomorrow.
Takeaway: 10 minutes of writing diagnosed the session more precisely than an hour of re-reading could.
example.walkthrough: Do a blank-page recall of the last lesson you studied, right now, before reading further.

pitfalls: Common trap: peeking 'just to get started' — the first peek converts recall into recognition and voids the diagnostic.
Common trap: recalling the easy parts — the blank page tempts you to write what you know; deliberately chase what you half-remember.
Common trap: no scoring — unexamined recall is journaling; score it against the source or it teaches nothing.
Common trap: too-large windows — recalling a whole month produces a blank page and despair; start with one session.
lessons.try_it: After your next study session, do a 10-minute blank-page recall and score it against the source.

lessons.title: Self-Quizzing Without Tools
concepts: You do not need an app to retrieve. Cover-and-recall (cover the page, say the content), question-in-margin (turn headings into questions), and teach-the-wall (explain aloud to an empty room) all work with zero tooling.
The question-in-margin technique: convert every heading into a question before reading the section, then answer it from memory after. Reading becomes a retrieval exercise with built-in feedback.
Teach-the-wall: explain the concept aloud as if to a smart beginner. Speaking forces linear, complete reconstruction — gaps you can skip in thought become audible stumbles in speech.
Interrogate with 'why' and 'how,' not 'what.' 'What is a mutex?' tests a definition; 'why does a mutex prevent race conditions, and when would you choose a semaphore instead?' tests understanding.
Make quizzing the default transition: every time you finish a section, close the material and quiz before moving on. The three minutes feel slow; they save hours of re-learning later.
