Common trap: no failure modes — 'it will just work' is not a defense; design the contingencies.
Common trap: defending without data — 'I feel spacing works for me' loses to 'missed day-ones → -12% accuracy.'
Common trap: never freezing 1.0 — perpetual drafting is procrastination; version, run, and revise from use.
lessons.try_it: Schedule your 10-minute capstone walkthrough — audience of at least one — and record it.

labs.title: Session audit: run the contract for a week
labs.objective: Test the two-party distraction contract in real sessions for seven days and measure what changes.
steps: Create ~/protocol/session-audit.md with columns: date, module, deep minutes, contract kept? (device rules), artifacts produced.
For seven days, run study sessions under the full contract: notifications off, phone in another room, one tab open, one module per session.
Log every session honestly — including the ones where you broke the contract and why.
Total your deep minutes and artifacts; compare against a normal week from memory.
Write a verdict paragraph: which half of the contract (yours) failed most, and the one fix you'll keep.

checks.hint: cat your session-audit.md and confirm artifacts (not hours) are logged per session.
Confirm seven days of entries exist (grep -c).

labs.title: Artifact audit: depth metrics on your last month
labs.objective: Apply depth metrics retroactively: inventory last month's artifacts vs. hours and set next month's artifact quota.
steps: List everything you produced last month that counts as an artifact: labs, proofs, projects, working systems, published notes.
Estimate the hours spent; compute nothing fancy — just place the two lists side by side in ~/protocol/artifact-audit.md.
Grade the month by the protocol's metric: what compounded (usable in the next module) vs. what evaporated?
Set next month's artifact quota: a specific number of specific artifact types — hours explicitly excluded from the target.
Print the audit and read the quota aloud; it should name artifacts, not hours.

checks.hint: cat artifact-audit.md and confirm the artifact quota names artifact types, not hours.
Confirm the artifact inventory lists concrete produced work.

labs.title: Sequence audit: map a dependency chain
labs.objective: Take an existing multi-module sequence and verify every module's prerequisites are satisfied by earlier modules.
steps: Pick a sequence you are studying (on this site or elsewhere) with at least 6 modules.
Create ~/sequences/audit.md listing each module and the concrete skills it assumes.
For each assumed skill, trace it to the earlier module that teaches it — mark any assumption with no source module as ORPHANED.
For every orphaned assumption, write the fix: promote it to a module, add a gate, or re-order.
Print the audit and count: modules, traced prerequisites, orphaned assumptions, proposed fixes.

checks.hint: cat your audit and confirm orphaned assumptions are marked (or explicitly zero).
Verify the file lists modules and traced prerequisites (grep -c).

labs.title: Build your own 6-module sequence
labs.objective: Backward-design a 6-module sequence on a topic you want to learn, with capstone, artifacts, and gates.
steps: Define the capstone artifact: what you will have built or be able to do at the end.
Work backward: list the dependency chain the capstone requires, in strict prerequisite order.
Compress or expand the chain to exactly 6 modules; each gets one lab artifact and one self-check gate.
Write the sequence to ~/sequences/my-sequence.md with the dependency rule stated at the bottom.
Delete-test: for each module, confirm which later module breaks without it; cut any module whose deletion breaks nothing.

checks.hint: cat my-sequence.md and confirm the capstone artifact is defined.
Confirm each module names its artifact and gate (grep for 'artifact').

labs.title: Attention ledger: instrument one week
labs.objective: Run the two-party distraction contract for seven days and measure what actually happens to your attention.
steps: Create ~/protocol/session-audit.md with columns: date, module, deep minutes, interruptions (with causes), contract kept? (device rules), artifacts produced.
For seven days, run every study session under the full contract: notifications off, phone in another room, one tab open, one module per session.
Log every session immediately afterward — including broken-contract sessions and why they broke.
Total your deep minutes and artifacts; compute interruptions per session and the top 3 causes.
Write a verdict paragraph: which half of the contract failed most, and the one system fix you will keep.

checks.hint: cat your session-audit.md and confirm deep minutes are logged per session.
grep for your verdict paragraph — the log must end in a decision, not just data.

labs.title: Build a 4-link mission sequence
labs.objective: Design and run a real 4-link sequence (modules → artifacts → handoffs → gate) on your current study topic.
steps: Pick one topic from your real study material and define the end artifact (e.g., '30 atomic cards loaded in the Leitner box').
Write ~/protocol/sequence-1.md with 4 links: each link names its module, its artifact, and its handoff to the next link.
Define the gate: the verifiable check that lets you advance (e.g., '30 cards exist, box has dated compartments').
Run links 1-2 this week; log handoffs as they happen.
Evaluate: did each link's output actually feed the next? Rewrite any fake handoff.

checks.hint: cat your sequence-1.md and confirm each link names its handoff.
grep for the gate definition — it must be verifiable, not 'understood the lesson'.

labs.title: Forgetting-curve experiment: the 24-hour review
labs.objective: Prove the forgetting curve to yourself: learn deeply, retrieve at 24 hours, and measure what the review saved.
steps: Pick 20 new items from your material; learn them with full attention and elaborative encoding (examples + connections).
Predict now: how many will you recall tomorrow with no review? Write the prediction in ~/protocol/forgetting-curve.md.
At 24 hours (no peeking before): blank-page recall all 20. Score against the source.
Re-study only the missed items, then run a second blank-page recall.
Write the verdict: predicted vs actual, and what the 24-hour retrieval saved versus your normal schedule.

checks.hint: cat your forgetting-curve.md and confirm the pre-registered prediction is there.
grep for the verdict comparing predicted vs actual recall.

labs.title: Schema map: skeleton-first learning
labs.objective: Build a one-page schema map for your hardest topic: skeleton first, details attached, then blank-page recall.
steps: Choose your hardest current topic and write its skeleton in ONE sentence at the top of ~/protocol/schema-map.md.
Attach 5-8 details as branches, each with its purpose ('sequence numbers → ordering').
Close the file. Blank-page recall: reproduce the skeleton, then each branch and purpose, from memory.
Score the recall; re-attach any branch that fell off.
Write one line: which detail had no skeleton hook before this lab (the one you kept forgetting)?

checks.hint: cat your schema-map.md and confirm the one-sentence skeleton is at the top.
grep for your blank-page recall score — the map must be tested, not just drawn.

labs.title: Blank-page recall session
labs.objective: Run three consecutive study→blank-page-recall→score cycles and log what the page diagnoses.
steps: Study one 25-minute module with full attention.
Close everything. Set a 10-minute timer; write everything you remember in ~/protocol/blank-page-1.md.
Score against the source: mark got / missed / distorted for each point.
Repeat for two more modules (blank-page-2.md, blank-page-3.md), each scored the same way.
Write the diagnosis: which miss type dominates (missed vs distorted), and tomorrow's retrieval targets.

checks.hint: ls ~/protocol/ and confirm three blank-page files exist.
grep for your miss-type diagnosis — misses and distortions need different fixes.

labs.title: Atomic flashcard deck: 30 cards
labs.objective: Build 30 atomic, production-prompt flashcards from your real material — and split every essay card.
steps: Create ~/protocol/deck.csv with columns: prompt, answer, source.
Write 30 cards: one fact per card, prompts that demand the exam's skill (why/how/when, not just what).
Run card surgery: flag any card needing a paragraph answer; split each into atomic cards until none remain.
Self-test 10 cards closed-book; log which prompts were ambiguous and rewrite them.
Write the count: cards created, cards split, ambiguous prompts fixed.

checks.hint: wc -l your deck.csv to verify the card count (header + cards).
grep for your card-surgery notes — every essay card must be split.

labs.title: Leitner box build and first cycle
labs.objective: Build a physical or digital 5-box Leitner system, load 20 cards, and run the first full review cycle.
steps: Build 5 boxes/compartments labeled 1-5 (shoebox dividers or app decks).
Load 20 atomic cards into box 1; photograph or screenshot the setup into ~/protocol/leitner.md with the date.
Run the review: box 1 daily; promote on correct recall, demote misses to box 1 — log every card's movement.
After 7 days, record the distribution: how many cards in each box.
Write the triage note: which box-1 cards are leeches (3+ misses) and need surgery.

checks.hint: cat your leitner.md and confirm the 7-day box distribution is logged.
grep for leech identification — box-1 churn must be triaged, not just observed.

labs.title: Leech surgery
labs.objective: Find your three worst leech cards and operate: split, rewrite, exemplify — then verify the repair.
steps: Identify 3 cards missed 5+ times (from your Leitner log or app stats); list them in ~/protocol/leech-surgery.md.
For each: diagnose WHY it fails (multi-part? vague prompt? no hook?).
Operate: split into atomic cards, rewrite prompts as production questions, add a concrete example or mnemonic to each.
Re-test the repaired cards after a 2-day delay; log the results.
Verdict: which surgery technique worked best (split vs rewrite vs mnemonic)? Keep it as a rule.

checks.hint: cat your leech-surgery.md and confirm each leech has a written diagnosis.
grep for the delayed re-test results — surgery without verification is hope.

labs.title: Zettelkasten starter: 20 atomic notes
labs.objective: Create 20 atomic, claim-titled, linked notes from your current material — no transcription allowed.
steps: Create ~/protocol/zettel/ and write 20 notes as separate .md files, one idea each, in your own words.
Title each file as a claim ('spacing-intervals-expand.md'), not a topic.
Add at least one real link per note to another note (supporting, contradicting, extending).
Run the stenographer test: delete any sentence that could have been copied verbatim from the source; rewrite it as thinking.
Write ~/protocol/zettel/index.md: the 5 most-connected notes and what the network reveals.

checks.hint: ls your zettel/ directory and count the note files — 20 minimum.
grep your index.md for the most-connected notes analysis.

labs.title: Weekly synthesis artifact
labs.objective: Produce a full weekly synthesis: memory-first draft, claims with evidence, open questions, archived.
steps: Close all notes. Draft ~/protocol/synthesis-week1.md from memory: what you learned this week.
Open your notes; check the draft. Mark every gap between draft and notes.
Rewrite as claims with evidence ('Day-one reviews are my highest-leverage habit: missed 3 → -12% accuracy').
End with 3 open questions — the things you understand least; these become next week's targets.
File in ~/protocol/syntheses/ with the date. This is the archive future weeks build on.

checks.hint: cat your synthesis and confirm claims carry evidence, not just summaries.
grep for the 3 open questions — a synthesis without confusions is incomplete.

labs.title: Environment friction audit and redesign
labs.objective: Audit your study environment's friction, redesign one high-leverage point, and measure the change.
steps: Write ~/protocol/friction-audit.md: list every distraction with its reach-cost (seconds to engage) and every study cue with its visibility.
Count pickups/interruptions in one baseline session; log the number.
Redesign ONE friction point: phone to another room, materials laid out, blockers on, 'in session' signal up.
Run three sessions in the redesigned environment; log pickups per session.
Verdict: baseline vs redesigned pickup counts, and the next friction point to fix.

checks.hint: cat your friction-audit.md and confirm distractions are listed with reach-costs.
grep for baseline vs redesigned pickup counts — the redesign must be measured.

labs.title: Designed session: plan, interval, shutdown
labs.objective: Run three fully-framed sessions (2-min plan, timed interval, real break, shutdown ritual) and compare to your norm.
steps: Before session 1, write the frame in ~/protocol/designed-sessions.md: what, why, target, interval length.
Run the interval; take the prescribed break (move, water, no screens).
Shutdown: what got done, what was missed, where to resume next time.
Repeat for sessions 2 and 3.
Compare: designed sessions vs your usual frameless sessions on deep minutes and artifacts — write the verdict.

checks.hint: cat your designed-sessions.md and confirm all three shutdowns are recorded.
grep for the designed-vs-frameless comparison verdict.

labs.title: Timed two-pass drill
labs.objective: Run a 20-scenario block under strict two-pass rules with a computed time budget and checkpoint discipline.
steps: Compute the budget (total minutes / 20, minus reserve) and write it at the top of ~/protocol/two-pass-drill.md.
First pass: answer confidently, eliminate-and-mark the rest, SKIP stuck ones (2x budget max).
Second pass: return to marked with fresh eyes; log which ones resolved.
Reserve: ordered review — marked first, then unsure, then mechanical scan for blanks.
Debrief: time adherence, checkpoint status, changes made with reasons, and the one tactic to keep.

checks.hint: cat your two-pass-drill.md and confirm the computed budget is written.
grep for the debrief — time adherence and change reasons must be logged.

labs.title: Error log + calibration predictions
labs.objective: Stand up the full metacognition stack: error log with root causes, prediction log, and a weekly cluster review.
steps: Create ~/protocol/error-log.md with columns: date, question/concept, picked vs correct, root cause type, fix.
Log your next 15 misses WITH root causes (gap / retrieval failure / misread / trap).
Before each scenario block, write a predicted score; after, the actual — in ~/protocol/predictions.md.
Cluster the 15 misses by root cause; name the top cluster and its systemic fix.
Re-test the top cluster after 5 days; mark entries CLOSED or re-open with a new fix.

checks.hint: cat your error-log.md and confirm root-cause types (not just answers) are logged.
grep for CLOSED entries — the log must verify fixes, not just list misses.

labs.title: Feynman explain-back recording
labs.objective: Record three 5-minute Feynman explain-backs (no jargon, no notes), log the stumbles, repair, and re-record.
steps: Pick your 3 shakiest concepts; record explain-back 1 of each (audio/video) into ~/protocol/feynman/.
Log every stumble, hand-wave, and jargon-crutch per recording in ~/protocol/feynman/stumbles.md.
Re-learn exactly the stumbled parts (different modality from the original learning).
Re-record each explain-back; the second take must be clean and simpler.
Verdict: which concept improved most, and what the stumbles revealed about your 'understanding.'

checks.hint: ls your feynman/ directory and confirm 6 recordings (3 first-takes + 3 re-takes).
grep your stumbles.md — every hand-wave must be logged as a gap.

labs.title: 48-hour countdown rehearsal
labs.objective: Rehearse the full 48-hour countdown against a mock exam: timeline, logistics, fuel protocol, and debrief.
steps: Write ~/protocol/countdown.md: your T-48h/T-24h/T-12h/T-2h timeline with specific times.
T-48h: last heavy session — after this, retrieval and light review only. Log the stop.
T-24h: logistics checklist completed (route, ID, timing, bag). Check each off in writing.
Sit the mock under exam conditions; run the first-10-minutes anxiety protocol and the ordered final review.
Within 24h: write the debrief (template from the lesson) — topics, surprises, protocol changes.

checks.hint: cat your countdown.md and confirm the four timeline checkpoints are specified.
grep for the post-mock debrief — the rehearsal is incomplete without it.

cheatsheet: Curriculum = attention delivery system. Engagement and attention are competing objectives.
Distraction-free by design: the missing features are missing deliberately.
Two-party contract: the site never distracts; you bring the device rules.
One module, one deep session. Session ends when the module ends.
Attention is trainable: targets ratchet up, boredom tolerance is practice.
Done = artifacts, not hours. Hours are input; artifacts compound.
Slow productivity: fewer obligations, natural pace, obsessive quality.

glossary.def: The five commitments shaping every track, module, and lab: distraction-free design, rhythm, attention training, depth metrics, pacing.
A measure of capability produced (artifacts), as opposed to input consumed (hours).
A produced unit of evidence: a completed lab, a re-derived proof, a working system, published notes.

The learner's half of the contract: notifications off, phone away, one tab open.

My study environment satisfies the device rules.

simulations.title: Why Did the Study Week Fail?
simulations.brief: You 'studied' 25 hours this week and failed the practice exam. Diagnose the protocol failure.

steps.symptom: 25 logged hours, practice exam score 52% (passing is 70%).
evidence: 18 hours re-reading notes, 5 hours highlighting, 2 hours practice questions
Can define terms, cannot apply them to new problems
No spaced intervals — everything crammed in 3 days
options: Not enough hours — push to 35 next week
Fluency illusion: re-reading and highlighting build recognition, not recall — the protocol optimized for the feeling of learning, and massed cramming guaranteed forgetting
steps.explain: Re-reading produces fluency (it feels known) without retrievability. The evidence: definitions without application. The protocol must swap recognition activities for retrieval activities and distribute them over time.

steps.symptom: You switch to practice questions. Scores rise to 64% but plateau. What's the missing mechanism?
evidence: Wrong answers re-read once, never re-tested
options: Error-driven spaced repetition: each misconception becomes a flashcard scheduled at expanding intervals until it's answered correctly three times cold
steps.explain: Plateaus come from uncorrected misconceptions. The fix is a system: errors → cards → spaced schedule → cold-correct ×3. Volume without an error loop just rehearses the same mistakes faster.

steps.symptom: New protocol designed. What single weekly metric proves it's working before the next exam?
evidence: Predicts exam performance, not just effort
options: Cold recall rate: percentage of due flashcards answered correctly with no hints, tracked weekly
steps.explain: Cold recall rate measures the actual asset (retrievable knowledge), not the input (hours) or the exhaust (notes). If it climbs 5% a week, the exam takes care of itself.

simulations.debrief: Study protocols fail on fluency (recognition ≠ recall), massing (cramming ≠ learning), and missing error loops. The fix: retrieval practice, spaced intervals, error cards, and one honest metric.

simulations.title: Choose the Method
simulations.brief: A brutal certification exam in 8 weeks. Four study methods compete for your 15 hours/week. Allocate like an engineer.

steps.text: 15 hrs/week, 8 weeks. Options: (A) video course end-to-end, (B) textbook cover-to-cover, (C) practice-exam-driven with targeted remediation, (D) study group discussions. Your allocation?

choices.label: A — videos feel productive and cover everything
choices.feedback: Videos are the re-reading of the digital age: high fluency, low retrieval. Eight weeks later you'll recognize everything and recall nothing under pressure.

choices.label: C — practice exams first, then remediate exactly what fails
choices.feedback: The exam is the specification: test early, let failures aim your studying, remediate with focused retrieval. Every hour targets a measured gap.

choices.label: B — the textbook is the complete source of truth
choices.feedback: Complete and unfinishable: 900 pages in 8 weeks at 15 hrs/week means skimming, and skimming means fluency without recall.

steps.text: Week 5: you've 'covered' 70% of the material but your first practice exam scores 58%. Panic is setting in. Repair?

choices.label: Speed up — finish the remaining 30% then do practice exams
choices.feedback: More coverage of the same passive method. The 58% isn't a coverage problem; it's a retrieval problem.

choices.label: Stop covering; switch to exam-driven remediation now — 3 weeks of targeted retrieval beats 3 weeks of finishing videos
choices.feedback: The correct late-stage pivot: abandon coverage, attack measured gaps. Triage beats completion.

steps.text: Week 5: practice scores 76% and climbing. But networking questions sit at 40% while everything else is 80%+. Your move?

choices.label: Keep the balanced rotation — it'll come up naturally
choices.feedback: The data names the gap; ignoring it is choosing to fail networking. Balanced feels fair; targeted wins.

choices.label: Reallocate: 60% of hours to networking until it hits 70%, maintenance reps for the rest
choices.feedback: Data-driven reallocation: attack the weakest link, maintain the rest with spaced reps. This is what the protocol is FOR.

simulations.debrief: Study like an engineer: the exam is the spec, practice tests are the test suite, failures are the bug reports, and your hours are the sprint capacity. Allocate to the red tests.

simulations.title: Build the Study Session
simulations.brief: Order the five moves of a 90-minute protocol study session.

steps.context: One 90-minute session, one topic. Order the moves for maximum durable learning.
items: Warm up with 10 minutes of cold recall on yesterday's material (no notes)
Attempt new problems BEFORE consulting references — struggle first
Check answers and convert every error into a spaced-repetition card
Do a 5-minute free-recall brain dump of the session's key ideas
Log the session: what was learned, what's still shaky, tomorrow's target

simulations.debrief: Recall before reference (warm-up), struggle before help (desirable difficulty), errors into cards (the loop), brain dump (consolidation), log (tomorrow's start). The session is a pipeline, not a vibe.

simulations.title: Audit the Study Plan
simulations.brief: A study plan for a certification exam has 3 protocol violations. Find them.

steps.config:
# study-plan.conf — 8 week cert prep
method = reread_notes            # line 2
schedule = cram_weekends          # line 3
retrieval = none                  # line 4
error_cards = 0                   # line 5
practice_exams = 1                # line 6
sleep = 5h                        # line 7
review = weekly                   # line 8

issues.description: Method is re-reading notes — pure fluency, zero retrieval. The plan optimizes for feeling prepared.
issues.fix: method = retrieval_practice (cold recall, practice questions, brain dumps).

issues.description: Crammed weekends — massed practice guarantees maximum forgetting between sessions.
issues.fix: schedule = distributed daily blocks with spaced intervals.

issues.description: No retrieval practice at all — the single highest-evidence study technique is entirely absent.
issues.fix: retrieval = every session starts with cold recall.

simulations.debrief: Lines 5–8 are also weak (no error cards, one practice exam, 5h sleep) but the three flagged lines are the structural violations: no retrieval, massed schedule, fluency-based method. Fix the method first.

simulations.title: Exam Week Triage
simulations.brief: The exam is in 72 hours. Your cold-recall rate is 68%; passing needs ~75%. Triage the final three days.

steps.text: 72 hours left. Cold recall 68%, need 75%. Your error cards cluster in two domains: subnetting (55%) and IAM policies (61%). Everything else is 75%+. The plan?

choices.label: Re-read all the notes once more for confidence
choices.feedback: Confidence without recall is how you walk in at 68% and walk out at 68%. The data is begging you to target.

choices.label: All retrieval, all gaps: drill subnetting and IAM cards at tight intervals, one full practice exam at hour 48, sleep 8h nightly
choices.feedback: The triage protocol: attack the measured gaps, verify with a full exam, protect sleep — the highest-ROI 72 hours available.

choices.label: Pull two all-nighters — more hours is more learning
choices.feedback: Sleep deprivation destroys exactly what the exam tests: recall under pressure. You'd trade 5 points of knowledge for 10 points of impairment.

steps.text: 24 hours left and you're exhausted, scoring 66% on drills — worse than three days ago. Emergency move?

choices.label: Caffeine and one more all-nighter — push through
choices.feedback: Pushing through impairment is how 68% becomes 60%. The exam punishes exactly this.

choices.label: Stop. Sleep 8 hours, light review only, trust the base — damage control beats more damage
choices.feedback: The least-bad move: sleep restores recall more than any cramming recovers. You sit the exam at your true 68% instead of an impaired 60%.

steps.text: Hour 48 practice exam: 77%. The gaps closed. Last 24 hours — what now?

choices.label: Learn a brand-new topic to 'maximize coverage'
choices.feedback: New topics at hour 48 create interference and anxiety. The exam rewards depth on the spec, not breadth beyond it.

choices.label: Light maintenance reps, review error cards once, pack your bag, sleep early — arrive at 100% of your 77%
choices.feedback: The professional finish: protect the gains, arrive rested. Exams are won in the 8 weeks before, and lost in the 24 hours before.

simulations.debrief: Exam-week triage: drill the measured gaps, verify with a full practice exam, protect sleep absolutely. The protocol's final lesson — performance is retrieval plus rest, and rest is not negotiable.

consoleSims.title: Organize the Study Archive
consoleSims.brief: Your study materials need archival order: a subjects directory, a protected error-log file, and locked permissions.

tasks.instruction: Create the file /home/user/study/error-log.txt — every misconception gets logged here.
Set mode 600 on /home/user/study/error-log.txt — your error log is private.
tasks.hint: Select the file, then chmod with mode 600.

consoleSims.debrief: The protocol needs infrastructure: a study directory, an error log with a name that reminds you what it's for, and permissions that keep it yours.

consoleSims.title: Run the Study Pipeline
consoleSims.brief: Treat your study week like a pipeline: trigger the week's run, retry the failed recall stage, configure the target, ship the review.

tasks.instruction: Trigger a new build — this week's study run.
The 'test' stage (Friday's cold-recall check) failed — retry it.
Approve the gated 'deploy' stage — publish the week's review notes.

consoleSims.debrief: The study week as CI: trigger (start), retry (re-drill failures), variables (declare targets), approve (publish the review). Green builds compound.

consoleSims.title: Triage the Blocker Queue
consoleSims.brief: Study blockers are incidents. Log them, assign them, move them — don't ruminate on them.

tasks.instruction: Create a P2 ticket titled 'Subnetting cold recall stuck at 55%'.
tasks.hint: New ticket: TITLE exactly as given, PRIORITY P2.

consoleSims.debrief: Externalize the blockers: a ticketed gap gets a plan; a ruminated gap gets anxiety. The queue is where stuck becomes scheduled.

consoleSims.title: Review the Notes Repo
consoleSims.brief: Your study notes live under version control. Branch the week's review, open the PR, and merge the corrections.

tasks.instruction: Open a PR titled 'Week 5: fix 6 misconception notes' from head 'review/week-5-corrections' to base 'main'.
tasks.hint: Open PR: exact title, BASE main, HEAD review/week-5-corrections.

tasks.instruction: Merge PR #1 (the pre-seeded one) — clear the queue before your review lands.
tasks.hint: In Pull requests, click Merge on PR #1.

consoleSims.debrief: Notes under version control: corrections are PRs, misconceptions get fixed with history, and the log shows exactly when each idea became correct.

terminalMissions.title: Start the Recall Log
terminalMissions.brief: Log cold-recall sessions to recall.txt — the protocol's honest instrument.

checks.hint: Type: echo "session1 recall 62pct" > recall.txt (no output on success).
Type: echo "session2 recall 68pct" >> recall.txt.
Type: cat recall.txt.

terminalMissions.success_message: Recall log started. What gets measured gets learned.

terminalMissions.title: Measure the Trend
terminalMissions.brief: Count sessions and search the log — is recall climbing?

checks.hint: Type: wc -l recall.txt.
Type: grep recall recall.txt.

terminalMissions.success_message: Trend measured. Climbing cold-recall is the only progress that counts.

terminalMissions.title: Seal the Target
terminalMissions.brief: Hash your exam-date target — commitment, tamper-evident.

checks.hint: Type: sha256sum recall-75 by exam day — the real hash plus your target are echoed.

terminalMissions.success_message: Target sealed. The protocol commits before the pressure arrives.

terminalMissions.title: Check the Session Edges

terminalMissions.success_message: Edges checked. Every review starts at the boundaries.

Type: echo $HOME.
